chapters.title: The Old Sea-dog at the Admiral Benbow
paragraphs: It was Squire Trelawney, Dr. Livesey, and the rest of the gentlemen who asked me to write down the whole story of Treasure Island, beginning to end — to hold nothing back but where the island lies, and that only because there is treasure still buried there. So I take up my pen in the year 17—, and go back to when my father kept the Admiral Benbow inn, and the brown old seaman with the sabre scar across his face first came to lodge under our roof.

I remember him as if it were yesterday, plodding up to the inn door with his sea-chest hauled behind him on a barrow — a tall, strong, heavy man, nut-brown, his tarry pigtail hanging over the shoulder of a grubby blue coat, his hands cracked and scarred with black, broken nails, and that sabre scar across one cheek, a dirty, livid white. I can still see him glancing round the cove and whistling to himself, then suddenly breaking into the old sea-song he would sing so often afterward:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

— in that high, cracked old voice that seemed to have been worn and broken at the capstan bars. Then he rapped on the door with a stick like a handspike that he carried, and when my father appeared he gruffly called for a glass of rum. When it came he drank it slowly, like a man who knew his liquor, lingering on the taste, his eyes still roving over the cliffs and up at our signboard.
“This is a handy cove,” he said at last, “and a pleasant spot for a tavern. Much custom, mate?”
My father told him no — very little, worse luck.

“Well then,” said he, “this is the berth for me. Here, matey,” he called to the man with the barrow, “bring her alongside and help up my chest. I’ll be staying a while,” he went on. “I’m a plain man — rum and bacon and eggs is what I want, and that headland up there to watch for ships. What to call me? You can call me captain. Oh, I see what you’re after — there.” And he flung three or four gold pieces down on the doorstep. “Tell me when I’ve drunk through that,” said he, with a look as fierce as any commander’s.

And indeed, ragged as his clothes were and rough as he talked, he looked nothing like a common hand who sailed before the mast — more like a mate or skipper used to being obeyed, or to hitting out. The man with the barrow told us the coach had set him down the morning before at the Royal George; that he had asked what inns there were along the coast; and that, hearing ours well spoken of and described as lonely, he had picked it over the rest for his lodging. That was all we ever learned about our guest.

He was a silent man by habit. All day he prowled the cove or the cliffs with a brass spyglass; all evening he sat in the corner of the parlour by the fire, drinking rum and water, very strong. Mostly he would not answer when spoken to — only glance up sharp and fierce and snort through his nose like a foghorn — and we and our regulars soon learned to leave him be. Every day, coming back from his walk, he would ask whether any seafaring men had passed along the road. At first we thought he asked for want of company of his own sort; in the end we saw it was the opposite — he wanted to avoid them. When a sailor did stop at the Admiral Benbow — as one did now and then, taking the coast road to Bristol — the captain would peer at him through the curtained door before coming into the parlour, and he was always quiet as a mouse while any such man was present. To me, at least, it was no mystery, for in a way I shared his fears. He had taken me aside one day and promised me a silver fourpenny on the first of every month if I would only keep my “weather-eye open for a seafaring man with one leg” and tell him the moment such a man appeared. Often enough, when the first of the month came round and I asked for my wages, he would only snort at me and stare me down; but before the week was out he was always sure to think better of it, bring me my fourpenny piece, and repeat his order to watch for “the seafaring man with one leg.”

I hardly need tell you how that figure haunted my dreams. On stormy nights, when the wind shook the four corners of the house and the surf roared in the cove and up the cliffs, I would see him in a thousand shapes, with a thousand devilish faces. Sometimes the leg was cut off at the knee, sometimes at the hip; sometimes he was a monstrous thing that had only ever had the one leg, set in the middle of his body. To watch him leap and run and chase me over hedge and ditch was the worst nightmare of all. So, one way and another, I paid pretty dear for my monthly fourpence, in the coin of these hideous dreams.

But frightened as I was by the idea of the one-legged sailor, I feared the captain himself far less than anyone else who knew him. There were nights he took more rum and water than his head could carry, and then he would sit singing his wicked old sea-songs, heeding nobody; but other nights he would call for drinks all round and force the whole trembling room to listen to his stories or join the chorus of his song. Many a time I have heard the house shaking with “Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum,” every neighbour joining in for dear life, in terror, each singing louder than the next to escape notice. For in these fits he was the most overbearing company you ever saw: he would slap the table for silence; he would fly into a rage at a question, or at no question at all, deciding the company was not following his tale; and he would let no one leave the inn until he had drunk himself sleepy and staggered off to bed.

It was his stories that frightened people most. Dreadful stories — hangings, walking the plank, storms at sea, the Dry Tortugas, and wild deeds and places on the Spanish Main. By his own telling he must have spent his life among some of the wickedest men ever let loose on the ocean, and the language he told it in shocked our plain country folk almost as much as the crimes he described. My father was forever sure the inn would be ruined — that people would stop coming to be bullied and crushed and sent shivering to bed — but I really believe his presence did us good. People were frightened at the time, yet looking back they rather liked it; it was a fine bit of excitement in a quiet country life. There was even a knot of younger men who claimed to admire him, calling him a “true sea-dog” and a “real old salt” and the like, and saying it was men like him that made England feared at sea.

In one way, though, he did fairly threaten to ruin us, for he stayed on week after week, and then month after month, until the money he had put down was long gone, and still my father never plucked up the heart to insist on more. If ever he hinted at it, the captain snorted through his nose so loudly it was almost a roar, and stared my poor father out of the room. I have seen him wringing his hands after such a rebuff, and I am sure the worry and the fright he lived in did much to hasten his early and unhappy death.

All the while he lodged with us the captain never changed his clothes, except to buy a few stockings from a pedlar. One side of his hat-brim came down, and he let it hang from that day on, for all the bother it gave him in a wind. I remember his coat, which he patched himself upstairs in his room until, toward the end, it was nothing but patches. He never wrote a letter or got one, and he spoke to nobody but the neighbours — and to them, mostly, only when the rum was in him. The great sea-chest none of us had ever seen open.

He was crossed only once, and that was near the end, when my poor father was far gone in the decline that carried him off. Dr. Livesey came late one afternoon to see the patient, took a little dinner from my mother, and went into the parlour to smoke a pipe while he waited for his horse to be brought down from the hamlet — we had no stable at the old Benbow. I followed him in, and I remember the contrast: the neat, bright doctor, his hair powdered snow-white, his black eyes quick, his manner pleasant, against the clumsy country people, and above all against that filthy, hulking, bleary scarecrow of a pirate of ours, slumped far gone in rum with his arms on the table. Suddenly the captain struck up his everlasting song:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum! Drink and the devil had done for the rest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

At first I had taken “the dead man’s chest” to mean that very box of his upstairs in the front room, and the thought had got tangled in my nightmares with the one-legged sailor. But by now we had all long stopped paying the song any mind; that night it was new to no one but Dr. Livesey, and I could see it did not please him, for he glanced up a moment, quite angry, before going on with what he was saying to old Taylor the gardener about a new cure for rheumatism. Meanwhile the captain warmed to his own music, and at last slapped the table in the way we all knew meant silence. Every voice stopped at once — all but the doctor’s, who went on as before, clear and kind, drawing briskly at his pipe between every word or two. The captain glared at him a while, slapped the table again, glared harder, and at last burst out with a vile, low oath: “Silence, there, between decks!”

“Were you speaking to me, sir?” said the doctor; and when the ruffian, with another oath, told him he was, “I have only one thing to say to you, sir,” the doctor replied: “that if you keep on drinking rum, the world will soon be rid of a very dirty scoundrel.”
The old fellow’s fury was terrible. He sprang up, drew and snapped open a sailor’s clasp-knife, and, balancing it open on his palm, threatened to pin the doctor to the wall.

The doctor never so much as stirred. He spoke to him just as before, over his shoulder, in the same tone — pitched a little high, so the whole room could hear — perfectly calm and steady: “If you do not put that knife back in your pocket this instant, I promise you, on my honour, you shall hang at the next assizes.”
Then came a battle of looks between them, but the captain soon gave in, put away his weapon, and sat back down, growling like a beaten dog.

“And now, sir,” the doctor went on, “since I know there is such a man in my district, you may count on it that I shall keep an eye on you day and night. I am not a doctor only — I am a magistrate; and if I catch one breath of complaint against you, even for a rudeness like tonight’s, I shall see to it you are hunted down and turned out of here. Let that be enough.”
Soon after, Dr. Livesey’s horse came to the door and he rode away; but the captain held his tongue that evening, and for many evenings to come.

chapters.title: Black Dog Appears and Disappears
paragraphs: It was not long after this that the first of the strange events occurred — the ones that finally rid us of the captain, though not, as you will see, of his affairs. It was a bitter winter, with long hard frosts and heavy gales, and from the first it was plain my poor father had little chance of seeing the spring. He sank day by day, and my mother and I had the whole inn on our hands, busy enough without sparing much thought for our unwelcome guest.

It was early one January morning — a pinching, frosty morning — the cove all grey with hoar-frost, the ripples lapping softly on the stones, the sun still low and only touching the hilltops and shining far out to sea. The captain had risen earlier than usual and gone off down the beach, his cutlass swinging under the broad skirts of the old blue coat, his brass spyglass under his arm, his hat tilted back on his head. I remember his breath trailing like smoke behind him as he strode away, and the last sound I heard of him as he rounded the big rock was a loud, indignant snort, as though his mind were still running on Dr. Livesey.

Well, mother was upstairs with father, and I was laying the breakfast table for the captain’s return, when the parlour door opened and in stepped a man I had never set eyes on before. He was a pale, waxy creature, short two fingers on the left hand, and though he wore a cutlass he did not look much of a fighter. I always kept an eye out for seafaring men, one leg or two, and I remember this one puzzled me: he was not quite sailorly, and yet there was a smack of the sea about him all the same.
I asked what he would have, and he said rum; but as I went to fetch it he sat down on a table and waved me closer. I stopped where I was, napkin in hand.
“Come here, sonny,” said he. “Come a bit nearer.”
I took a step toward him.
“Is this table here set out for my mate Bill?” he asked, with a kind of leer.
I told him I knew no mate Bill — the table was for a man staying with us whom we called the captain.

“Well,” said he, “my mate Bill might well be called the captain, like as not. He has a cut on one cheek, and a mighty pleasant way with him, especially in drink, has my mate Bill. Let us say, for argument’s sake, that your captain has a cut on one cheek — and let us say, if you like, that it is the right cheek. Ah, there you are. Now — is my mate Bill in this house?”
I told him he was out walking.
“Which way, sonny? Which way is he gone?”

And when I had pointed out the rock, and told him how and how soon the captain was likely to be back, and answered a question or two more, “Ah,” said he, “this’ll be as good as a drink to my mate Bill.”

The look on his face as he said it was anything but pleasant, and I had my own reasons to think the stranger was mistaken, even if he meant what he said. But it was no business of mine, I thought, and besides it was hard to know what to do. The stranger kept lurking just inside the inn door, peering round the corner like a cat watching a mouse. Once I stepped out into the road myself, but he called me straight back, and when I did not move fast enough to suit him, a horrible change came over that waxy face and he ordered me in with an oath that made me jump. The moment I was back he turned smooth again, half fawning, half sneering, patted my shoulder and told me I was a good lad and he had taken quite a fancy to me. “I have a son of my own,” he said, “the very spit of you, and he is all the pride of my heart. But the great thing for boys is discipline, sonny — discipline. Now, if you had sailed with Bill, you’d not have stood there to be spoken to twice — not you. That was never Bill’s way, nor the way of them as sailed with him. And here, sure enough, is my mate Bill, with a spyglass under his arm, bless his old heart. You and me’ll just step back into the parlour, sonny, and get behind the door, and we’ll give Bill a little surprise — bless his heart, I say again.”

With that the stranger backed into the parlour with me and put me behind him in the corner, both of us hidden by the open door. I was very uneasy and alarmed, as you may imagine, and it did nothing for my nerves to see that the stranger was plainly frightened himself. He freed the hilt of his cutlass and loosened the blade in its sheath, and the whole time we waited he kept swallowing as if he had what we used to call a lump in the throat.
At last in strode the captain, slammed the door behind him without a glance to either side, and marched straight across the room to where his breakfast was waiting.
“Bill,” said the stranger, in a voice he seemed to force loud and bold.

The captain spun on his heel and faced us. All the brown had drained from his face; even his nose had gone blue. He had the look of a man seeing a ghost, or the devil, or something worse, if worse there is; and upon my word, I felt sorry to watch him turn, in a moment, so old and sick.
“Come, Bill — you know me; you know an old shipmate, surely, Bill,” said the stranger.
The captain gave a sort of gasp.
“Black Dog!” said he.

“And who else?” said the other, easier now. “Black Dog as ever was, come to see his old shipmate Billy at the Admiral Benbow inn. Ah, Bill, Bill, we have seen a deal of life, us two, since I lost these two talons,” — and he held up his maimed hand.
“Now look here,” said the captain. “You’ve run me to ground; here I am; well then — out with it; what is it?”

“That’s you, Bill,” said Black Dog. “You’re in the right of it, Billy. I’ll have a glass of rum from this dear child I’ve taken such a liking to, and we’ll sit down, if you please, and talk straight, like old shipmates.”

When I came back with the rum, the two were already seated on either side of the captain’s breakfast — Black Dog next the door, sitting sideways so as to keep one eye on his old shipmate and one, I thought, on his line of retreat.
He told me to go out and leave the door standing wide. “None of your keyholes for me, sonny,” he said; and I left the two of them together and slipped back to the bar.
For a long time, though I certainly did my best to listen, I could make out nothing but a low murmur; but at last the voices rose, and I could pick up a word or two, mostly oaths, from the captain.
“No, no, no, no — and there’s an end of it!” he cried once; and again, “If it comes to swinging, let all swing, says I.”

Then all at once came a great burst of oaths and other noise — chair and table went over together, a clash of steel followed, then a cry of pain, and the next moment I saw Black Dog in full flight and the captain hard after him, both with drawn cutlasses, Black Dog streaming blood from the left shoulder. Right at the door the captain aimed one last tremendous slash, which would surely have split him to the backbone had it not caught on the big signboard of the Admiral Benbow. You can see the notch on the lower edge of the frame to this day.

That blow ended the fight. Once out on the road, Black Dog, wound and all, showed a wonderful clean pair of heels and was over the brow of the hill in half a minute. The captain, for his part, stood staring at the signboard like a man dazed. Then he passed his hand over his eyes again and again, and at last turned back indoors.
“Jim,” said he, “rum.” And as he spoke he swayed a little, and caught himself with one hand against the wall.
“Are you hurt?” cried I.
“Rum,” he said again. “I must get away from here. Rum! Rum!”

I ran for it, but I was so shaken by all that had happened that I broke a glass and jammed the tap, and while I was still fumbling I heard a heavy fall in the parlour, and running in, found the captain stretched full length on the floor. At the same moment my mother, alarmed by the shouting and the fighting, came hurrying down to help. Between us we lifted his head. He was breathing very loud and hard, but his eyes were shut and his face a dreadful colour.
“Dear, deary me,” cried my mother, “what a disgrace on the house — and your poor father lying sick upstairs!”

Meanwhile we had no notion how to help the captain, nor any thought but that he had got his death-wound in the scuffle with the stranger. I fetched the rum, sure enough, and tried to get it down his throat, but his teeth were clenched and his jaws as strong as iron. It was a blessed relief when the door opened and Doctor Livesey came in, on his visit to my father.
“Oh, doctor,” we cried, “what are we to do? Where is the man hurt?”

“Hurt? Rubbish!” said the doctor. “No more hurt than you or I. The man has had a stroke, just as I warned him. Now, Mrs. Hawkins, run up to your husband and, if you can, tell him nothing of this. For my part, I must do my best to save this fellow’s three-times-worthless life. Jim, fetch me a basin.”

When I got back with the basin the doctor had already slit the captain’s sleeve and laid bare his great sinewy arm, tattooed in several places. “Here’s luck,” “A fair wind,” and “Billy Bones his fancy” were lettered very neat and clear along the forearm; and up near the shoulder was a sketch of a gallows with a man hanging from it — done, I thought, with great spirit.

“Prophetic,” said the doctor, touching the picture with his finger. “And now, Master Billy Bones — if that is your name — we’ll have a look at the colour of your blood. Jim,” he said, “are you afraid of blood?”
“No, sir,” said I.
“Well then,” said he, “you hold the basin.” And with that he took his lancet and opened a vein.

A great deal of blood was taken before the captain opened his eyes and looked round him, bleary. First he made out the doctor, with an unmistakable scowl; then his eye fell on me, and he looked relieved. But all at once his colour changed, and he struggled to sit up, crying, “Where’s Black Dog?”

“There is no Black Dog here,” said the doctor, “except the one on your own back. You have been drinking rum, and you have had a stroke, exactly as I told you; and I have just this minute, much against my will, hauled you headfirst out of the grave. Now, Mr. Bones—”
“That’s not my name,” he broke in.

“Much I care,” said the doctor. “It’s the name of a buccaneer I’ve heard of, and I shall call you by it for short. Here is what I have to say to you: one glass of rum won’t kill you, but if you take one you’ll take another, and another, and I stake my wig that if you don’t break off short you’ll die — do you understand? Die. And go to your own place, like the man in the Bible. Come now, make the effort. I’ll help you to your bed this once.”
Between us, with no end of trouble, we got him upstairs and laid him on his bed, where his head fell back on the pillow as if he were near to fainting.
“Now, mind you,” said the doctor, “I clear my conscience — the name of rum, for you, is death.”
And with that he set off to see my father, drawing me along by the arm.

“This is nothing,” he said the moment he had shut the door. “I have drawn blood enough to keep him quiet a while; he should lie a week where he is — that is best for him and for you — but another stroke would settle him.”

chapters.title: The Black Spot
paragraphs: About noon I came to the captain’s door with some cooling drinks and his medicine. He was lying much as we had left him, only propped a little higher, and he looked both weak and worked-up.

“Jim,” he said, “you’re the only one here worth anything, and you know I’ve always been good to you. Never a month but I gave you your silver fourpenny. And now, mate, you see I’m pretty low, and deserted by all; so, Jim, you’ll bring me one mug of rum — won’t you, matey?”
“The doctor—” I began.

But he broke in, cursing the doctor in a feeble voice but heartily. “Doctors is all swabs,” he said; “and that one there — what does he know about seafaring men? I’ve been in places hot as pitch, with mates dropping round me of Yellow Jack, and the good land heaving like the sea with earthquakes — what does the doctor know of country like that? I lived on rum, I tell you. It’s been meat and drink to me, and man and wife besides; and if I can’t have my rum now I’m a poor old hulk on a lee shore. My blood’ll be on you, Jim, and on that swab of a doctor.” And he ran on cursing a while. “Look, Jim, how my fingers won’t keep still,” he went on, pleading now. “I can’t hold ’em steady, not I. I’ve not had a drop this whole blessed day. That doctor’s a fool, I tell you. If I don’t get a dram of rum, Jim, I’ll have the horrors — I’ve seen some of ’em already. I saw old Flint, there in the corner behind you, plain as print; and if I get the horrors, I’m a man that’s lived rough, and I’ll raise Cain. Your own doctor said one glass wouldn’t hurt me. I’ll give you a golden guinea for a mug, Jim.”

He was growing more and more excited, and it frightened me for my father, who was very low that day and needed quiet; besides, the doctor’s words, now thrown back at him, had reassured me, and I was rather offended at being offered a bribe.
“I want no money of yours,” said I, “only what you owe my father. I’ll bring you one glass, and not another.”
When I brought it to him he snatched it greedily and drank it off.
“Aye, aye,” said he, “that’s a sight better, sure enough. And now, matey, did that doctor say how long I’m to lie here in this old berth?”
“A week at least,” said I.

“Thunder!” he cried. “A week! I can’t do that — they’d have the black spot on me by then. The lubbers are casting about to get word of me this very minute — lubbers that couldn’t keep what they had, and now want to grab what is another man’s. Is that seamanly behaviour, now, I ask you? But I’m a saving soul. I never wasted good money of mine, nor lost it either; and I’ll trick ’em again. I’m not afraid of ’em. I’ll shake out another reef, matey, and leave ’em standing.”

As he spoke he had hauled himself up off the bed with great difficulty, gripping my shoulder so hard I nearly cried out, and dragging his legs like dead weight. His words, bold as they were in meaning, made a sad contrast with the feeble voice that carried them. He paused once he had got himself sitting on the edge.
“That doctor’s done for me,” he muttered. “My ears are singing. Lay me back.”
Before I could do much to help, he had dropped back to where he had been, and lay a while in silence.
“Jim,” he said at length, “you saw that seafaring man today?”
“Black Dog?” I asked.

“Ah — Black Dog,” said he. “He’s a bad one; but there’s worse behind him that put him on. Now, if I can’t get clear no way, and they tip me the black spot, mind you — it’s my old sea-chest they’re after. You get on a horse — you can ride, can’t you? Well then, you get on a horse and go to — yes, I will! — to that everlasting swab of a doctor, and tell him to pipe all hands, magistrates and such, and he’ll lay ’em aboard at the Admiral Benbow — all old Flint’s crew, every man and boy of ’em that’s left. I was first mate, I was — old Flint’s first mate — and I’m the only one as knows the place. He gave it me at Savannah, when he lay a-dying, like as I might now, you see. But you’ll not breathe a word unless they tip me the black spot, or unless you see that Black Dog again, or a seafaring man with one leg, Jim — him above all.”
“But what is the black spot, captain?” I asked.
“A summons, mate. I’ll tell you if they bring it. But you keep your weather-eye open, Jim, and I’ll share with you, fair halves, upon my honour.”

He rambled on a little longer, his voice growing weaker; but soon after I had given him his medicine — which he took like a child, with the remark, “If ever a sailor needed drugs, it’s me” — he fell at last into a heavy, swoon-like sleep, and I left him so. What I should have done if all had gone well I do not know. Most likely I should have told the doctor the whole story, for I was in mortal fear the captain might regret his confidences and make an end of me. But as it fell out, my poor father died quite suddenly that evening, and that pushed everything else aside. Our natural grief, the neighbours’ visits, the arranging of the funeral, and all the inn’s work to be carried on in the meantime kept me so busy that I had scarcely time to think of the captain, far less to be afraid of him.

He did get downstairs the next morning, to be sure, and ate his meals as usual, though little, and took, I am afraid, more than his share of rum, helping himself at the bar, scowling and snorting, with nobody daring to cross him. The night before the funeral he was as drunk as ever, and it was shocking, in that house of mourning, to hear him bawling out his ugly old sea-song; but weak as he was, we all went in fear of him, and the doctor had been called away suddenly to a case many miles off and never came near the house after my father’s death. I have said the captain was weak, and indeed he seemed to grow weaker rather than mend. He hauled himself up and down stairs, and went from the parlour to the bar and back, and now and then put his nose out of doors to smell the sea, holding to the walls for support as he went and breathing hard and fast like a man climbing a steep hill. He never spoke to me directly, and it is my belief he had as good as forgotten what he had confided; but his temper was flightier, and — allowing for his bodily weakness — more violent than ever. He had an alarming new way, when drunk, of drawing his cutlass and laying it bare on the table before him. Yet for all that, he took less notice of people, and seemed shut up in his own thoughts, and rather wandering. Once, for instance, to our great surprise, he struck up a different tune — a kind of country love-song he must have learned in his youth, before he took to the sea.

So things went until, the day after the funeral — about three o’clock of a bitter, foggy, frosty afternoon — I was standing a moment at the door, full of sad thoughts of my father, when I saw someone coming slowly along the road. He was plainly blind, for he tapped ahead of him with a stick and wore a great green shade over his eyes and nose; and he was bent, as if with age or weakness, and wrapped in a huge old tattered sea-cloak with a hood that made him look positively deformed. I never in my life saw a more dreadful-looking figure. He stopped a little short of the inn and, raising his voice in an odd sing-song, called out to the air in front of him: “Will any kind friend tell a poor blind man, who has lost the precious sight of his eyes in the gracious defence of his native country, England — and God bless King George! — where, or in what part of the country, he may now be?”
“This is the Admiral Benbow, at Black Hill Cove, my good man,” I told him.
“I hear a voice,” said he — “a young one. Give me your hand, my kind young friend, and lead me inside.”

I held out my hand, and the horrible, soft-spoken, eyeless creature gripped it in a moment like a vice. I was so startled that I tried to pull away, but with one motion of his arm the blind man dragged me close.
“Now, boy,” said he, “take me in to the captain.”
“Sir,” said I, “upon my word I dare not.”
“Oh,” he sneered, “that’s it, is it? Take me in straight, or I’ll break your arm.”
And as he spoke he gave it a wrench that made me cry out.
“Sir,” said I, “it is for your own sake. The captain is not what he used to be. He sits with a drawn cutlass. Another gentleman—”

“Come, now — march,” he cut in; and I never heard a voice so cruel and cold and ugly as that blind man’s. It cowed me more than the pain, and I began to obey him at once, walking straight in at the door and toward the parlour, where our sick old buccaneer sat, dazed with rum. The blind man clung to me, gripping me in one iron fist and leaning more of his weight on me than I could well carry. “Lead me straight up to him, and when I’m in sight, call out, ‘Here’s a friend for you, Bill.’ If you don’t, I’ll do this” — and he gave me a twist that I thought would have made me faint. Between this and that, I was so utterly terrified of the blind beggar that I forgot my dread of the captain, and as I opened the parlour door I called out the words he had ordered, in a trembling voice.

The poor captain looked up, and at one glance the rum went clean out of him and left him staring sober. His face showed not so much terror as mortal sickness. He made a movement to rise, but I do not believe he had the strength left in his body.

“Stay where you are, Bill,” said the beggar. “Blind I may be, but I can hear a finger stir. Business is business. Put out your left hand. Boy — take him by the wrist and bring his left hand over to my right.”
We both obeyed him to the letter, and I saw him pass something from the hollow of the hand that held his stick into the captain’s palm, which closed on it at once.

“And now that’s done,” said the blind man; and with the words he suddenly let go of me and, with astonishing speed and sureness, skipped out of the parlour and into the road, where, as I still stood frozen, I could hear his stick go tap-tap-tapping off into the distance.

It was some time before either of us came to his senses; but at last, and about at the same moment, I let go his wrist, which I was still holding, and he drew in his hand and looked sharply at the palm.
“Ten o’clock!” he cried. “Six hours — we’ll beat ’em yet,” and he sprang to his feet.
Even as he did, he reeled, put his hand to his throat, stood swaying a moment, and then, with an odd sound, fell his whole height face-first to the floor.

I ran to him at once, calling for my mother. But all haste was useless. The captain had been struck dead by a thundering stroke. It is a strange thing to account for, since I had certainly never liked the man — though of late I had begun to pity him — but the moment I saw he was dead, I burst into a flood of tears. It was the second death I had known, and the grief of the first was still fresh in my heart.

chapters.title: The Sea-chest
paragraphs: I lost no time, of course, in telling my mother all that I knew — and perhaps should have told her long before — and we saw ourselves at once in a difficult and dangerous position. Some of the man’s money, if he had any, was certainly due to us, but it was not likely that our captain’s shipmates, above all the two specimens I had seen, Black Dog and the blind beggar, would be inclined to give up their booty in payment of the dead man’s debts. The captain’s order to mount at once and ride for Doctor Livesey would have left my mother alone and unprotected, which was not to be thought of. Indeed, it seemed impossible for either of us to remain much longer in the house. The fall of coals in the kitchen grate, the very ticking of the clock, filled us with alarms. The neighbourhood, to our ears, seemed haunted by approaching footsteps; and what between the dead body of the captain on the parlour floor and the thought of that detestable blind beggar hovering near at hand and ready to return, there were moments when, as the saying goes, I jumped in my skin for terror. Something must speedily be decided, and it occurred to us at last to go out together and seek help in the neighbouring hamlet. No sooner said than done. Bare-headed as we were, we ran out at once into the gathering evening and the frosty fog.

The hamlet lay not many hundred yards away, though out of sight, on the other side of the next cove; and what greatly encouraged me, it was in an opposite direction from that from which the blind man had appeared and to which he had presumably returned. We were not many minutes on the road, though we sometimes stopped to take hold of each other and listen. But there was no unusual sound — nothing but the low wash of the ripple and the croaking of the inhabitants of the wood.

It was already candle-light when we reached the hamlet, and I shall never forget how much I was cheered to see the yellow shine in doors and windows; but that, as it turned out, was the best of the help we were likely to get in that quarter. For — you would have thought men would have been ashamed of themselves — no soul would agree to return with us to the Admiral Benbow. The more we told of our troubles, the more — man, woman, and child — they clung to the shelter of their houses. The name of Captain Flint, though strange to me, was well enough known to some there and carried a great weight of terror. Some of the men who had been to field-work on the far side of the Admiral Benbow remembered, besides, having seen several strangers on the road, and taking them for smugglers, had bolted away; and one at least had seen a little lugger in what we called Kitt’s Hole. For that matter, anyone who was a comrade of the captain’s was enough to frighten them to death. And the short and the long of the matter was that, while we could get several who were willing enough to ride to Dr. Livesey’s, which lay in another direction, not one would help us defend the inn.

They say cowardice is infectious; but then argument is, on the other hand, a great emboldener. And so, when each had said his say, my mother made them a speech. She would not, she declared, lose money that belonged to her fatherless boy. “If none of the rest of you dare,” she said, “Jim and I dare. Back we will go, the way we came, and small thanks to you big, hulking, chicken-hearted men. We’ll have that chest open, if we die for it. And I’ll thank you for that bag, Mrs. Crossley, to bring back our lawful money in.”

Of course I said I would go with my mother, and of course they all cried out at our foolhardiness, but even then not a man would go along with us. All they would do was give me a loaded pistol in case we were attacked, and promise to have horses ready saddled in case we were pursued on our return, while one lad was to ride forward to the doctor’s in search of armed assistance.

My heart was beating finely when we two set out into the cold night upon this dangerous venture. A full moon was beginning to rise and peered redly through the upper edges of the fog, and this increased our haste, for it was plain, before we came forth again, that all would be as bright as day, and our departure exposed to the eyes of any watchers. We slipped along the hedges, noiseless and swift, and neither saw nor heard anything to increase our terrors, until, to our relief, the door of the Admiral Benbow had closed behind us.

I slipped the bolt at once, and we stood and panted for a moment in the dark, alone in the house with the dead captain’s body. Then my mother got a candle in the bar, and holding each other’s hands, we advanced into the parlour. He lay as we had left him, on his back, with his eyes open and one arm stretched out.

“Draw down the blind, Jim,” whispered my mother; “they might come and watch outside. And now,” said she when I had done so, “we have to get the key off _that;_ and who’s to touch it, I should like to know!” and she gave a kind of sob as she said the words.

I went down on my knees at once. On the floor close to his hand there was a little round of paper, blackened on one side. I could not doubt that this was the _black spot;_ and taking it up, I found written on the other side, in a very good, clear hand, this short message: “You have till ten tonight.”
“He had till ten, Mother,” said I; and just as I said it, our old clock began striking. This sudden noise startled us shockingly; but the news was good, for it was only six.
“Now, Jim,” she said, “that key.”

I felt in his pockets, one after another. A few small coins, a thimble, and some thread and big needles, a piece of pigtail tobacco bitten away at the end, his clasp-knife with the crooked handle, a pocket compass, and a tinder box — that was all they contained, and I began to despair.
“Perhaps it’s round his neck,” suggested my mother.

Overcoming a strong repugnance, I tore open his shirt at the neck, and there, sure enough, hanging on a bit of tarry string, which I cut with his own clasp-knife, we found the key. At this triumph we were filled with hope and hurried upstairs without delay to the little room where he had slept so long and where his box had stood since the day of his arrival.
It was like any other seaman’s chest on the outside, the initial “B” burned on the top of it with a hot iron, and the corners somewhat smashed and broken as by long, rough usage.
“Give me the key,” said my mother; and though the lock was very stiff, she had turned it and thrown back the lid in a twinkling.

A strong smell of tobacco and tar rose from the interior, but nothing was to be seen on the top except a suit of very good clothes, carefully brushed and folded. They had never been worn, my mother said. Under that, the miscellany began — a quadrant, a tin canikin, several sticks of tobacco, two brace of very handsome pistols, a piece of bar silver, an old Spanish watch and some other trinkets of little value and mostly of foreign make, a pair of compasses mounted with brass, and five or six curious West Indian shells. I have often wondered since why he should have carried these shells about with him in his wandering, guilty, and hunted life.

In the meantime, we had found nothing of any value except the silver and the trinkets, and neither of these were in our line. Underneath there was an old boat-cloak, whitened with sea-salt on many a harbour-bar. My mother pulled it up impatiently, and there lay before us the last things in the chest: a bundle tied up in oilcloth, looking like papers, and a canvas bag that gave forth, at a touch, the jingle of gold.

“I’ll show these rogues that I’m an honest woman,” said my mother. “I’ll have my dues, and not a farthing over. Hold Mrs. Crossley’s bag.” And she began to count over the amount of the captain’s score from the sailor’s bag into the one I was holding.

It was a long, difficult business, for the coins were of all countries and sizes — doubloons, and louis d’ors, and guineas, and pieces of eight, and I know not what else besides, all shaken together at random. The guineas, too, were about the scarcest, and it was with these only that my mother knew how to make her count.

When we were about halfway through, I suddenly put my hand on her arm, for I had heard in the silent frosty air a sound that brought my heart into my mouth — the tap-tapping of the blind man’s stick upon the frozen road. It drew nearer and nearer, while we sat holding our breath. Then it struck sharp on the inn door, and then we could hear the handle being turned and the bolt rattling as the wretched being tried to enter; and then there was a long time of silence both within and without. At last the tapping started up again, and, to our indescribable joy and gratitude, died slowly away again until it could no longer be heard.

“Mother,” said I, “take the whole and let’s be going,” for I was sure the bolted door must have seemed suspicious and would bring the whole hornet’s nest about our ears; though how thankful I was that I had bolted it, none could tell who had never met that terrible blind man.

But my mother, frightened as she was, would not consent to take a fraction more than was due to her, and was obstinately unwilling to be content with less. It was not yet seven, she said, by a long way; she knew her rights and she would have them; and she was still arguing with me when a little low whistle sounded a good way off upon the hill. That was enough, and more than enough, for both of us.
“I’ll take what I have,” she said, jumping to her feet.
“And I’ll take this to square the count,” said I, picking up the oilskin packet.

Next moment we were both groping downstairs, leaving the candle by the empty chest; and the next we had opened the door and were in full retreat. We had not started a moment too soon. The fog was rapidly dispersing; already the moon shone quite clear on the high ground on either side; and it was only in the exact bottom of the dell and round the tavern door that a thin veil still hung unbroken to conceal the first steps of our escape. Far less than halfway to the hamlet, very little beyond the bottom of the hill, we would have to come out into the moonlight. Nor was this all, for the sound of several footsteps running already reached our ears, and as we looked back in their direction, a light tossing to and fro and still rapidly advancing showed that one of the newcomers carried a lantern.
“My dear,” said my mother suddenly, “take the money and run on. I am going to faint.”

This was certainly the end for both of us, I thought. How I cursed the cowardice of the neighbours; how I blamed my poor mother for her honesty and her greed, for her past foolhardiness and present weakness! We were just at the little bridge, by good fortune; and I helped her, tottering as she was, to the edge of the bank, where, sure enough, she gave a sigh and fell on my shoulder. I do not know how I found the strength to do it at all, and I am afraid it was roughly done, but I managed to drag her down the bank and a little way under the arch. Farther I could not move her, for the bridge was too low to let me do more than crawl below it. So there we had to stay — my mother almost entirely exposed and both of us within earshot of the inn.

chapters.title: The Last of the Blind Man
paragraphs: My curiosity, in a way, was stronger than my fear, for I could not stay where I was, but crept back to the bank again, where, sheltering my head behind a bush of broom, I might watch the road in front of our door. I was barely in position before my enemies began to arrive — seven or eight of them, running hard, their feet beating out of time along the road, and the man with the lantern some paces in front. Three men ran together, hand in hand; and I made out, even through the mist, that the middle man of the trio was the blind beggar. The next moment his voice confirmed I was right.
“Down with the door!” he cried.

“Aye, aye, sir!” answered two or three; and a rush was made upon the Admiral Benbow, the lantern-bearer following; and then I could see them pause, and hear speeches passed in a lower key, as if they were surprised to find the door open. But the pause was brief, for the blind man again issued his commands. His voice sounded louder and higher, as if he were on fire with eagerness and rage.
“In, in, in!” he shouted, and cursed them for their delay.
Four or five of them obeyed at once, two remaining on the road with the formidable beggar. There was a pause, then a cry of surprise, and then a voice shouting from the house, “Bill’s dead.”
But the blind man swore at them again for their delay.
“Search him, some of you shirking lubbers, and the rest of you aloft and get the chest,” he cried.

I could hear their feet rattling up our old stairs, so that the house must have shook with it. Promptly afterwards, fresh sounds of astonishment arose; the window of the captain’s room was thrown open with a slam and a jingle of broken glass, and a man leaned out into the moonlight, head and shoulders, and called down to the blind beggar on the road below him.
“Pew,” he cried, “they’ve been before us. Someone’s turned the chest out from top to bottom.”
“Is it there?” roared Pew.
“The money’s there.”
The blind man cursed the money.
“Flint’s fist, I mean,” he cried.
“We don’t see it here nohow,” returned the man.
“Here, you below there, is it on Bill?” cried the blind man again.
At that another fellow, probably the one who had stayed below to search the captain’s body, came to the door of the inn. “Bill’s been overhauled a’ready,” said he; “nothin’ left.”

“It’s these people of the inn — it’s that boy. I wish I had put his eyes out!” cried the blind man, Pew. “There were no time ago — they had the door bolted when I tried it. Scatter, lads, and find ’em.”
“Sure enough, they left their glim here,” said the fellow from the window.
“Scatter and find ’em! Rout the house out!” reiterated Pew, striking with his stick upon the road.

Then there followed a great commotion through all our old inn, heavy feet pounding to and fro, furniture thrown over, doors kicked in, until the very rocks re-echoed and the men came out again, one after another, on the road and declared that we were nowhere to be found. And just the same whistle that had alarmed my mother and me over the dead captain’s money was once more clearly audible through the night, but this time twice repeated. I had thought it to be the blind man’s trumpet, so to speak, summoning his crew to the assault, but I now realised it was a signal from the hillside towards the hamlet, and from its effect upon the buccaneers, a signal to warn them of approaching danger.
“There’s Dirk again,” said one. “Twice! We’ll have to budge, mates.”

“Budge, you skulk!” cried Pew. “Dirk was a fool and a coward from the first — you wouldn’t mind him. They must be close by; they can’t be far; you have your hands on it. Scatter and look for them, dogs! Oh, shiver my soul,” he cried, “if I had eyes!”

This appeal seemed to produce some effect, for two of the fellows began to look here and there among the lumber, but half-heartedly, I thought, and with half an eye to their own danger all the time, while the rest stood irresolute on the road.

“You have your hands on thousands, you fools, and you hang a leg! You’d be as rich as kings if you could find it, and you know it’s here, and you stand there skulking. There wasn’t one of you dared face Bill, and I did it — a blind man! And I’m to lose my chance for you! I’m to be a poor, crawling beggar, sponging for rum, when I might be rolling in a coach! If you had the pluck of a weevil in a biscuit you would catch them still.”
“Hang it, Pew, we’ve got the doubloons!” grumbled one.
“They might have hid the blessed thing,” said another. “Take the Georges, Pew, and don’t stand here squalling.”

Squalling was the word for it; Pew’s anger rose so high at these objections that at last, his passion completely taking the upper hand, he struck at them right and left in his blindness and his stick sounded heavily on more than one.
These, in their turn, cursed back at the blind miscreant, threatened him in horrid terms, and tried in vain to catch the stick and wrest it from his grasp.

This quarrel was the saving of us, for while it was still raging, another sound came from the top of the hill on the side of the hamlet — the tramp of horses galloping. Almost at the same time a pistol-shot, flash and report, came from the hedge side. And that was plainly the last signal of danger, for the buccaneers turned at once and ran, separating in every direction, one seaward along the cove, one slant across the hill, and so on, so that in half a minute not a sign of them remained but Pew. Him they had deserted — whether in sheer panic or out of revenge for his ill words and blows, I do not know — but there he remained behind, tapping up and down the road in a frenzy, and groping and calling for his comrades. Finally he took a wrong turn and ran a few steps past me, towards the hamlet, crying, “Johnny, Black Dog, Dirk,” and other names, “you won’t leave old Pew, mates — not old Pew!”
Just then the noise of horses topped the rise, and four or five riders came in sight in the moonlight and swept at full gallop down the slope.

At this Pew saw his error, turned with a scream, and ran straight for the ditch, into which he rolled. But he was on his feet again in a second and made another dash, now utterly bewildered, right under the nearest of the oncoming horses.

The rider tried to save him, but in vain. Down went Pew with a cry that rang high into the night; and the four hoofs trampled and spurned him and passed by. He fell on his side, then gently collapsed on his face, and moved no more.

I leapt to my feet and hailed the riders. They were pulling up, in any case, horrified at the accident; and I soon saw who they were. One, trailing behind the rest, was the lad who had gone from the hamlet to Dr. Livesey’s; the rest were revenue officers, whom he had met on the way, and with whom he had had the intelligence to return at once. Some news of the lugger in Kitt’s Hole had found its way to Supervisor Dance and set him out that night in our direction, and to that circumstance my mother and I owed our preservation from death.

Pew was dead, stone dead. As for my mother, when we had carried her up to the hamlet, a little cold water and salts soon brought her round again, and she was none the worse for her terror, though she still continued to lament the balance of the money. In the meantime the supervisor rode on, as fast as he could, to Kitt’s Hole; but his men had to dismount and grope down the dingle, leading, and sometimes supporting, their horses, and in continual fear of ambushes; so it was no great matter for surprise that when they got down to the Hole the lugger was already under way, though still close in. He hailed her. A voice replied, telling him to keep out of the moonlight or he would get some lead in him, and at the same time a bullet whistled close by his arm. Soon after, the lugger doubled the point and disappeared. Mr. Dance stood there, as he said, “like a fish out of water,” and all he could do was to dispatch a man to B—— to warn the cutter. “And that,” said he, “is just about as good as nothing. They’ve got off clean, and there’s an end. Only,” he added, “I’m glad I trod on Master Pew’s corns,” for by this time he had heard my story.

I went back with him to the Admiral Benbow, and you cannot imagine a house in such a state of smash; the very clock had been thrown down by these fellows in their furious hunt after my mother and me; and though nothing had actually been taken away except the captain’s money-bag and a little silver from the till, I could see at once that we were ruined. Mr. Dance could make nothing of the scene.
“They got the money, you say? Well, then, Hawkins, what in fortune were they after? More money, I suppose?”
“No, sir; not money, I think,” I replied. “In fact, sir, I believe I have the thing in my breast pocket; and to tell you the truth, I should like to get it put somewhere safe.”
“To be sure, boy; quite right,” said he. “I’ll take it, if you like.”
“I thought perhaps Dr. Livesey—” I began.

“Perfectly right,” he interrupted very cheerily, “perfectly right — a gentleman and a magistrate. And, now I come to think of it, I might as well ride round there myself and report to him or the squire. Master Pew’s dead, when all’s done; not that I regret it, but he’s dead, you see, and people will make it out against an officer of his Majesty’s revenue, if make it out they can. Now, I’ll tell you, Hawkins, if you like, I’ll take you along.”
I thanked him heartily for the offer, and we walked back to the hamlet where the horses were. By the time I had told mother of my purpose, they were all in the saddle.
“Dogger,” said Mr. Dance, “you have a good horse; take up this lad behind you.”
As soon as I was mounted, holding on to Dogger’s belt, the supervisor gave the word, and the party struck out at a bouncing trot on the road to Dr. Livesey’s house.

chapters.title: The Captain’s Papers
paragraphs: We rode hard all the way until we drew up before Dr. Livesey’s door. The house was all dark to the front.
Mr. Dance told me to jump down and knock, and Dogger gave me a stirrup to climb down by. The door was opened almost at once by the maid.
“Is Dr. Livesey in?” I asked.
No, she said, he had come home in the afternoon but had gone up to the hall to dine and pass the evening with the squire.
“So there we go, boys,” said Mr. Dance.

This time, since the distance was short, I did not mount, but ran with Dogger’s stirrup-leather to the lodge gates and up the long, leafless, moonlit avenue to where the white line of the hall buildings looked on either hand on great old gardens. Here Mr. Dance dismounted, and taking me along with him, was admitted at a word into the house.

The servant led us down a matted passage and showed us at the end into a great library, all lined with bookcases and busts on top of them, where the squire and Dr. Livesey sat, pipe in hand, on either side of a bright fire.

I had never seen the squire so near at hand. He was a tall man, over six feet high, and broad in proportion, and he had a bluff, rough-and-ready face, all roughened and reddened and lined by his long travels. His eyebrows were very black, and moved readily, and this gave him a look of some temper — not bad, you would say, but quick and high.
“Come in, Mr. Dance,” says he, very stately and condescending.
“Good evening, Dance,” says the doctor with a nod. “And good evening to you, friend Jim. What good wind brings you here?”

The supervisor stood up straight and stiff and told his story like a lesson; and you should have seen how the two gentlemen leaned forward and looked at each other, and forgot to smoke in their surprise and interest. When they heard how my mother went back to the inn, Dr. Livesey fairly slapped his thigh, and the squire cried “Bravo!” and broke his long pipe against the grate. Long before it was done, Mr. Trelawney (that, you will remember, was the squire’s name) had got up from his seat and was striding about the room, and the doctor, as if to hear better, had taken off his powdered wig and sat there looking very strange indeed with his own close-cropped black head.
At last Mr. Dance finished the story.

“Mr. Dance,” said the squire, “you are a very noble fellow. And as for riding down that black, atrocious miscreant, I regard it as an act of virtue, sir, like stamping on a cockroach. This lad Hawkins is a trump, I see. Hawkins, will you ring that bell? Mr. Dance must have some ale.”
“And so, Jim,” said the doctor, “you have the thing they were after, have you?”
“Here it is, sir,” said I, and gave him the oilskin packet.
The doctor looked it all over, as if his fingers were itching to open it; but instead of doing that, he put it quietly in the pocket of his coat.

“Squire,” said he, “when Dance has had his ale he must, of course, be off on his Majesty’s service; but I mean to keep Jim Hawkins here to sleep at my house, and with your permission, I propose we should have up the cold pie and let him sup.”
“As you will, Livesey,” said the squire; “Hawkins has earned better than cold pie.”
So a big pigeon pie was brought in and put on a side-table, and I made a hearty supper, for I was as hungry as a hawk, while Mr. Dance was further complimented and at last dismissed.
“And now, squire,” said the doctor.
“And now, Livesey,” said the squire in the same breath.
“One at a time, one at a time,” laughed Dr. Livesey. “You have heard of this Flint, I suppose?”

“Heard of him!” cried the squire. “Heard of him, you say! He was the bloodthirstiest buccaneer that sailed. Blackbeard was a child to Flint. The Spaniards were so prodigiously afraid of him that, I tell you, sir, I was sometimes proud he was an Englishman. I’ve seen his topsails with these eyes, off Trinidad, and the cowardly son of a rum-puncheon I sailed with put back — put back, sir, into Port of Spain.”
“Well, I’ve heard of him myself, in England,” said the doctor. “But the point is, did he have money?”
“Money!” cried the squire. “Have you heard the story? What were these villains after but money? What do they care for but money? For what would they risk their rascal carcasses but money?”

“That we shall soon know,” replied the doctor. “But you are so confoundedly hot-headed and exclamatory that I cannot get a word in. What I want to know is this: supposing that I have here in my pocket some clue to where Flint buried his treasure, will that treasure amount to much?”

“Amount, sir!” cried the squire. “It will amount to this: if we have the clue you talk about, I fit out a ship in Bristol dock, and take you and Hawkins here along, and I’ll have that treasure if I search a year.”
“Very well,” said the doctor. “Now, then, if Jim is agreeable, we’ll open the packet”; and he laid it before him on the table.
The bundle was sewn together, and the doctor had to get out his instrument case and cut the stitches with his medical scissors. It contained two things — a book and a sealed paper.
“First of all we’ll try the book,” observed the doctor.

The squire and I were both peering over his shoulder as he opened it, for Dr. Livesey had kindly motioned me to come round from the side-table, where I had been eating, to enjoy the sport of the search. On the first page there were only some scraps of writing, such as a man with a pen in his hand might make for idleness or practice. One was the same as the tattoo mark, “Billy Bones his fancy”; then there was “Mr. W. Bones, mate,” “No more rum,” “Off Palm Key he got itt,” and some other snatches, mostly single words and unintelligible. I could not help wondering who it was that had “got itt,” and what “itt” was that he got. A knife in his back, as likely as not.
“Not much instruction there,” said Dr. Livesey as he moved on.

The next ten or twelve pages were filled with a curious series of entries. There was a date at one end of the line and at the other a sum of money, as in common account-books, but instead of explanatory writing, only a varying number of crosses between the two. On the 12th of June, 1745, for instance, a sum of seventy pounds had plainly become due to someone, and there was nothing but six crosses to explain the cause. In a few cases, to be sure, the name of a place would be added, as “Offe Caraccas,” or a mere entry of latitude and longitude, as “62o 17′ 20″, 19o 2′ 40″.”

The record lasted over nearly twenty years, the amount of the separate entries growing larger as time went on, and at the end a grand total had been made out after five or six wrong additions, with these words appended: “Bones, his pile.”
“I can’t make head or tail of this,” said Dr. Livesey.

“The thing is as clear as noonday,” cried the squire. “This is the black-hearted hound’s account-book. These crosses stand for the names of ships or towns that they sank or plundered. The sums are the scoundrel’s share, and where he feared an ambiguity, you see he added something clearer. ‘Offe Caraccas,’ now; you see, here was some unhappy vessel boarded off that coast. God help the poor souls that manned her — coral long ago.”
“Right!” said the doctor. “See what it is to be a traveller. Right! And the amounts increase, you see, as he rose in rank.”
There was little else in the volume but a few bearings of places noted in the blank leaves towards the end and a table for reducing French, English, and Spanish moneys to a common value.
“Thrifty man!” cried the doctor. “He wasn’t the one to be cheated.”
“And now,” said the squire, “for the other.”

The paper had been sealed in several places with a thimble by way of seal — the very thimble, perhaps, that I had found in the captain’s pocket. The doctor opened the seals with great care, and there fell out the map of an island, with latitude and longitude, soundings, names of hills and bays and inlets, and every particular that would be needed to bring a ship to a safe anchorage on its shores. It was about nine miles long and five across, shaped, you might say, like a fat dragon standing up, and had two fine land-locked harbours, and a hill in the centre part marked “The Spy-glass.” There were several additions of a later date, but above all, three crosses of red ink — two on the north part of the island, one in the southwest — and beside this last, in the same red ink, and in a small, neat hand, very different from the captain’s tottery characters, these words: “Bulk of treasure here.”
Over on the back the same hand had written this further information:
Tall tree, Spy-glass shoulder, bearing a point to the N. of N.N.E.
Skeleton Island E.S.E. and by E.
Ten feet.
The bar silver is in the north cache; you can find it by the trend of the east hummock, ten fathoms south of the black crag with the face on it.
The arms are easy found, in the sand-hill, N. point of north inlet cape, bearing E. and a quarter N. J.F.
That was all; but brief as it was, and incomprehensible to me, it filled the squire and Dr. Livesey with delight.

“Livesey,” said the squire, “you will give up this wretched practice at once. Tomorrow I start for Bristol. In three weeks’ time — three weeks! — two weeks — ten days — we’ll have the best ship, sir, and the choicest crew in England. Hawkins shall come as cabin-boy. You’ll make a famous cabin-boy, Hawkins. You, Livesey, are ship’s doctor; I am admiral. We’ll take Redruth, Joyce, and Hunter. We’ll have favourable winds, a quick passage, and not the least difficulty in finding the spot, and money to eat, to roll in, to play duck and drake with ever after.”
“Trelawney,” said the doctor, “I’ll go with you; and I’ll go bail for it, so will Jim, and be a credit to the undertaking. There’s only one man I’m afraid of.”
“And who’s that?” cried the squire. “Name the dog, sir!”

“You,” replied the doctor; “for you cannot hold your tongue. We are not the only men who know of this paper. These fellows who attacked the inn tonight — bold, desperate blades, for sure — and the rest who stayed aboard that lugger, and more, I dare say, not far off, are, one and all, through thick and thin, bound that they’ll get that money. None of us must go alone until we get to sea. Jim and I shall stick together in the meantime; you’ll take Joyce and Hunter when you ride to Bristol, and from first to last, not one of us must breathe a word of what we’ve found.”
“Livesey,” returned the squire, “you are always in the right of it. I’ll be as silent as the grave.”

chapters.title: I Go to Bristol
paragraphs: It took longer than the squire expected before we were ready for the sea, and none of our first plans—not even Dr. Livesey's plan of keeping me beside him—could be carried out as we intended. The doctor had to go to London to find a physician to take over his practice; the squire was hard at work at Bristol; and I lived on at the hall under the charge of old Redruth, the gamekeeper, almost a prisoner, but full of sea-dreams and the most delightful expectations of strange islands and adventures. I brooded for hours at a time over the map, every detail of which I remembered well. Sitting by the fire in the housekeeper's room, I approached that island in my imagination from every possible direction; I explored every acre of its surface; I climbed a thousand times to that tall hill they call the Spy-glass, and from the top enjoyed the most wonderful and changing views. Sometimes the isle was thick with savages, with whom we fought, sometimes full of dangerous animals that hunted us, but in all my fancies nothing occurred to me as strange and tragic as our actual adventures.

So the weeks passed on, till one fine day a letter arrived addressed to Dr. Livesey, with this added note, “To be opened, in the case of his absence, by Tom Redruth or young Hawkins.” Obeying this order, we found, or rather I found—for the gamekeeper was a poor hand at reading anything but print—the following important news:
_Old Anchor Inn, Bristol, March 1, 17—._
Dear Livesey—As I do not know whether you are at the hall or still in London, I am sending this in duplicate to both places.
The ship is bought and fitted out. She lies at anchor, ready for sea. You never imagined a sweeter schooner—a child could sail her—two hundred tons; name, HISPANIOLA.

I got her through my old friend, Blandly, who has proven himself throughout to be the most surprising trump. The admirable fellow literally slaved on my behalf, and so, I may say, did everyone in Bristol, as soon as they got wind of the port we were sailing for—treasure, I mean.
“Redruth,” I said, interrupting the letter, “Dr. Livesey will not like that. The squire has been talking, after all.”
“Well, who has a better right?” growled the gamekeeper. “A pretty rum go if the squire isn't allowed to talk for Dr. Livesey, I should think.”
At that I gave up all attempts at commentary and read straight on:

Blandly himself found the HISPANIOLA, and by the most admirable management got her for the merest trifle. There is a class of men in Bristol monstrously prejudiced against Blandly. They go so far as to declare that this honest creature would do anything for money, that the HISPANIOLA belonged to him, and that he sold her to me at an absurdly high price—the most transparent slanders. None of them dare, however, to deny the merits of the ship.
So far there was not a hitch. The workmen, to be sure—riggers and the rest—were most annoyingly slow; but time cured that. It was the crew that troubled me.

I wanted a full twenty men—in case of natives, buccaneers, or the odious French—and I had the devil's own trouble finding so much as half a dozen, until the most remarkable stroke of fortune brought me the very man I needed.

I was standing on the dock when, by the merest accident, I fell into conversation with him. I found that he was an old sailor, kept a public-house, knew all the seafaring men in Bristol, had lost his health ashore, and wanted a good berth as cook to get back to sea again. He had hobbled down there that morning, he said, just to get a smell of the salt.

I was monstrously touched—so would you have been—and, out of pure pity, I hired him on the spot to be ship's cook. Long John Silver, he is called, and has lost a leg; but I regarded that as a recommendation, since he lost it in his country's service, under the immortal Hawke. He has no pension, Livesey. Imagine the abominable age we live in!

Well, sir, I thought I had only found a cook, but it was a crew I had discovered. Between Silver and myself we got together in a few days a company of the toughest old salts imaginable—not pretty to look at, but fellows, by their faces, of the most indomitable spirit. I declare we could fight a frigate.
Long John even got rid of two out of the six or seven I had already hired. He showed me in a moment that they were just the sort of fresh-water swabs we had to fear on an adventure of importance.

I am in the most magnificent health and spirits, eating like a bull, sleeping like a tree, yet I shall not enjoy a moment until I hear my old tarpaulins tramping round the capstan. Seaward, ho! Hang the treasure! It's the glory of the sea that has turned my head. So now, Livesey, come post-haste; do not lose an hour, if you respect me.
Let young Hawkins go at once to see his mother, with Redruth for a guard; and then both come full speed to Bristol. John Trelawney

_Postscript._—I did not tell you that Blandly, who, by the way, is to send a consort after us if we don't turn up by the end of August, had found an admirable fellow for sailing master—a stiff man, which I regret, but in all other respects a treasure. Long John Silver unearthed a very competent man for a mate, a man named Arrow. I have a boatswain who pipes, Livesey; so things shall go man-o'-war fashion on board the good ship HISPANIOLA.

I forgot to tell you that Silver is a man of substance; I know of my own knowledge that he has a banker's account, which has never been overdrawn. He leaves his wife to manage the inn; and as she is a woman of colour, a pair of old bachelors like you and I may be excused for guessing that it is the wife, quite as much as the health, that sends him back to roving. J. T.
P.P.S.—Hawkins may stay one night with his mother. J. T.

You can imagine the excitement that letter put me in. I was half beside myself with glee; and if ever I despised a man, it was old Tom Redruth, who could do nothing but grumble and lament. Any of the under-gamekeepers would gladly have changed places with him; but such was not the squire's pleasure, and the squire's pleasure was like law among them all. Nobody but old Redruth would have dared even to grumble.

The next morning he and I set out on foot for the Admiral Benbow, and there I found my mother in good health and spirits. The captain, who had so long been a cause of so much discomfort, was gone where the wicked cease from troubling. The squire had had everything repaired, and the public rooms and the sign repainted, and had added some furniture—above all a beautiful armchair for mother in the bar. He had also found her a boy as an apprentice so that she would not lack help while I was gone.

It was on seeing that boy that I understood, for the first time, my situation. Up to that moment I had thought about the adventures before me, not at all of the home I was leaving; and now, at the sight of this clumsy stranger, who was to stay here in my place beside my mother, I had my first attack of tears. I am afraid I led that boy a dog's life, for as he was new to the work, I had a hundred opportunities of setting him right and putting him down, and I was not slow to take advantage of them.

The night passed, and the next day, after dinner, Redruth and I were afoot again and on the road. I said good-bye to Mother and the cove where I had lived since I was born, and the dear old Admiral Benbow—since he was repainted, no longer quite so dear. One of my last thoughts was of the captain, who had so often strode along the beach with his cocked hat, his sabre-cut cheek, and his old brass telescope. Next moment we had turned the corner and my home was out of sight.

The mail coach picked us up about dusk at the Royal George on the heath. I was wedged in between Redruth and a stout old gentleman, and in spite of the swift motion and the cold night air, I must have dozed a great deal from the very first, and then slept like a log up hill and down dale through stage after stage, for when I was woken at last it was by a punch in the ribs, and I opened my eyes to find that we were standing still in front of a large building on a city street and that the day had already broken a long time ago.
“Where are we?” I asked.
“Bristol,” said Tom. “Get down.”

Mr. Trelawney had taken up his residence at an inn far down the docks to oversee the work on the schooner. We had now to walk there, and our way, to my great delight, lay along the quays and beside the great multitude of ships of all sizes and rigs and nations. On one, sailors were singing at their work; on another, there were men aloft, high over my head, hanging onto threads that seemed no thicker than a spider's. Though I had lived by the shore all my life, I seemed never to have been near the sea until then. The smell of tar and salt was something new. I saw the most wonderful figureheads, that had all been far across the ocean. I saw, besides, many old sailors, with rings in their ears, and whiskers curled in ringlets, and tarry pigtails, and their swaggering, clumsy sea-walk; and if I had seen as many kings or archbishops I could not have been more delighted.
And I was going to sea myself, to sea in a schooner, with a piping boatswain and pig-tailed singing seamen, to sea, bound for an unknown island, and to hunt for buried treasure!

While I was still lost in this delightful dream, we came suddenly to the front of a large inn and met Squire Trelawney, all dressed out like a sea-officer in stout blue cloth, coming out of the door with a smile on his face and a capital imitation of a sailor's walk.
“Here you are,” he cried, “and the doctor came last night from London. Bravo! The ship's company is complete!”
“Oh, sir,” I cried, “when do we sail?”
“Sail!” says he. “We sail tomorrow!”

chapters.title: At the Sign of the Spy-glass
paragraphs: When I had finished breakfast, the squire gave me a note addressed to John Silver at the sign of the Spy-glass, and told me I would easily find the place by following the line of the docks and keeping a sharp lookout for a little tavern with a large brass telescope for a sign. I set off, overjoyed at the chance to see more of the ships and seamen, and I picked my way through a great crowd of people and carts and bales, since the dock was now at its busiest hour, until I found the tavern in question.

It was a bright enough little place. The sign was newly painted, the windows had neat red curtains, and the floor was cleanly sanded. There was a street on each side and an open door on both, which made the large, low room fairly clear to see in, despite the clouds of tobacco smoke.
The customers were mostly seafaring men, and they talked so loudly that I hung at the door, almost afraid to enter.

As I was waiting, a man came out of a side room, and at a single glance I was certain he must be Long John. His left leg was cut off close by the hip, and under his left shoulder he carried a crutch, which he managed with wonderful dexterity, hopping about on it like a bird. He was very tall and strong, with a face as big as a ham—plain and pale, but intelligent and smiling. Indeed, he seemed in the most cheerful spirits, whistling as he moved among the tables, with a merry word or a slap on the shoulder for the more favoured of his guests.

Now, to tell you the truth, from the very first mention of Long John in Squire Trelawney's letter I had taken a fear in my mind that he might turn out to be the very one-legged sailor whom I had watched for so long at the old Benbow. But one look at the man before me was enough. I had seen the captain, and Black Dog, and the blind man Pew, and I thought I knew what a buccaneer was like—a very different creature, in my view, from this clean and pleasant-tempered landlord.
I plucked up courage at once, crossed the threshold, and walked straight up to the man where he stood, propped on his crutch, talking to a customer.
“Mr. Silver, sir?” I asked, holding out the note.
“Yes, my lad,” said he. “That is my name, to be sure. And who may you be?” Then, as he saw the squire's letter, he seemed to me to give something almost like a start.
“Oh!” said he, quite loud, and offering his hand. “I see. You are our new cabin-boy. Pleased I am to see you.”
And he took my hand in his large firm grasp.

Just then one of the customers on the far side rose suddenly and made for the door. It was close beside him, and he was out in the street in a moment. But his hurry had caught my notice, and I recognized him at a glance. It was the tallow-faced man, missing two fingers, who had been the first to come to the Admiral Benbow.
“Oh!” I cried. “Stop him! It's Black Dog!”
“I don't care two coppers who he is,” cried Silver. “But he hasn't paid his bill. Harry, run and catch him.”
One of the others, who was nearest the door, leaped up and started in pursuit.
“If he were Admiral Hawke he shall pay his bill,” cried Silver. Then, releasing my hand, he asked, “Who did you say he was? Black what?”
“Dog, sir,” said I. “Has Mr. Trelawney not told you of the buccaneers? He was one of them.”
“So?” cried Silver. “In my house! Ben, run and help Harry. One of those swabs, was he? Was that you drinking with him, Morgan? Step up here.”
The man whom he called Morgan—an old, grey-haired, mahogany-faced sailor—came forward pretty sheepishly, rolling his quid of tobacco.
“Now, Morgan,” said Long John very sternly, “you never clapped eyes on that Black—Black Dog before, did you, now?”
“Not I, sir,” said Morgan with a salute.
“You didn't know his name, did you?”
“No, sir.”

“By the powers, Tom Morgan, it's as well for you!” exclaimed the landlord. “If you had been mixed up with the likes of that, you would never have set another foot in my house, you may lay to that. And what was he saying to you?”
“I don't rightly know, sir,” answered Morgan.

“Do you call that a head on your shoulders, or a blessed dead-eye?” cried Long John. “Don't rightly know, don't you! Perhaps you don't happen to rightly know who you were speaking to, perhaps? Come now, what was he jawing about—voyages, captains, ships? Pipe up! What was it?”
“We was a-talking of keel-hauling,” answered Morgan.
“Keel-hauling, was you? And a mighty suitable thing too, and you may lay to that. Get back to your seat for a lubber, Tom.”

And then, as Morgan rolled back to his place, Silver added to me in a confidential whisper that was very flattering, I thought: “He's quite an honest man, Tom Morgan, only stupid. And now,” he ran on again aloud, “let's see—Black Dog? No, I don't know the name, not I. Yet I kind of think I've—yes, I've seen the swab. He used to come in here with a blind beggar, he used.”
“That he did, you may be sure,” said I. “I knew that blind man too. His name was Pew.”

“It was!” cried Silver, now quite excited. “Pew! That were his name for certain. Ah, he looked a shark, he did! If we run down this Black Dog now, there'll be news for Cap'n Trelawney! Ben's a good runner; few seamen run better than Ben. He should run him down, hand over hand, by the powers! He talked of keel-hauling, did he? I'll keel-haul him!”

All the while he was jerking out these phrases he was stumping up and down the tavern on his crutch, slapping tables with his hand, and putting on such a show of excitement as would have convinced an Old Bailey judge or a Bow Street runner. My suspicions had been thoroughly reawakened on finding Black Dog at the Spy-glass, and I watched the cook closely. But he was too deep, and too quick, and too clever for me, and by the time the two men had come back out of breath and confessed that they had lost the track in a crowd, and been scolded like thieves, I would have gone bail for the innocence of Long John Silver.
