“See here now, Hawkins,” said he, “here's a blessed hard thing on a man like me, now, isn't it? There's Cap'n Trelawney—what's he to think? Here I have this confounded son of a Dutchman sitting in my own house drinking my own rum! Here you come and tell me of it plain, and here I let him give us all the slip before my blessed deadlights! Now, Hawkins, you do me justice with the cap'n. You're a lad, you are, but you're as smart as paint. I see that when you first come in. Now, here it is: what could I do, with this old timber I hobble on? When I was an A B master mariner I'd have come up alongside of him, hand over hand, and broached him to in a brace of old shakes, I would; but now—”
And then, all of a sudden, he stopped, and his jaw dropped as though he had remembered something.
“The bill!” he burst out. “Three goes of rum! Why, shiver my timbers, if I hadn't forgotten my own bill!”
And dropping onto a bench, he laughed until the tears ran down his cheeks. I could not help joining in, and we laughed together, peal after peal, until the tavern rang again.

“Why, what a precious old sea-calf I am!” he said at last, wiping his cheeks. “You and me should get on well, Hawkins, for I'll take my oath I should be rated ship's boy. But come now, stand by to go about. This won't do. Duty is duty, messmates. I'll put on my old cockerel hat, and step along with you to Cap'n Trelawney, and report this affair. For mind you, it's serious, young Hawkins; and neither you nor me has come out of it with what I should make so bold as to call credit. Nor you neither, says you; not smart—none of the pair of us smart. But dash my buttons! That was a good one about my bill.”
And he began to laugh again, and so heartily that, though I did not see the joke as he did, I was once more obliged to join him in his mirth.

On our short walk along the quays, he made himself the most interesting companion, telling me about the different ships we passed, their rig, tonnage, and nationality, explaining the work that was going on—how one was discharging, another taking in cargo, and a third making ready for sea—and every now and then telling me some little anecdote of ships or seamen or repeating a nautical phrase till I had learned it perfectly. I began to see that here was one of the best shipmates anyone could hope for.
When we got to the inn, the squire and Dr. Livesey were seated together, finishing a quart of ale with a toast in it, before they went aboard the schooner on a visit of inspection.

Long John told the story from first to last, with a great deal of spirit and the most perfect truth. “That was how it were, now, weren't it, Hawkins?” he would say now and again, and I could always back him entirely.
The two gentlemen regretted that Black Dog had got away, but we all agreed there was nothing to be done, and after he had been complimented, Long John took up his crutch and departed.
“All hands aboard by four this afternoon,” shouted the squire after him.
“Aye, aye, sir,” cried the cook, in the passage.
“Well, squire,” said Dr. Livesey, “I don't put much faith in your discoveries, as a general thing; but I will say this—John Silver suits me.”
“The man's a perfect trump,” declared the squire.
“And now,” added the doctor, “Jim may come on board with us, may he not?”
“To be sure he may,” says the squire. “Take your hat, Hawkins, and we'll see the ship.”

chapters.title: Powder and Arms
paragraphs: The Hispaniola lay some distance out, and we rowed under the figureheads and around the sterns of many other ships, their cables sometimes scraping beneath our keel and sometimes swinging above us. At last we came alongside, and as we stepped aboard we were met and greeted by the mate, Mr. Arrow, a weathered old sailor with gold earrings and a squint. He and the squire got along famously, thick as old friends from the first moment, but I soon noticed that things were not the same between Mr. Trelawney and the captain.

The captain was a sharp-featured man who seemed irritated with everything on board, and we were about to learn why, for we had barely made our way down into the cabin when a sailor appeared at the door.
“Captain Smollett, sir, asking to speak with you,” said he.
“I am always at the captain’s orders. Show him in,” said the squire.
The captain, who was close behind his messenger, entered at once and shut the door behind him.
“Well, Captain Smollett, what have you to say? All well, I hope; all shipshape and seaworthy?”

“Well, sir,” said the captain, “I think it’s better to speak plain, even at the risk of giving offence. I don’t like this voyage; I don’t like the men; and I don’t like my officer. That’s it in short.”
“Perhaps, sir, you don’t like the ship?” the squire asked, visibly angry.
“I can’t say as to that, sir, not having put her through her paces yet,” said the captain. “She seems a capable craft; that’s the most I can say.”
“Possibly, sir, you may not like your employer, either?” said the squire.
But here Dr. Livesey stepped in.

“Hold on,” said he, “hold on. Questions like that only stir up ill feeling. The captain has either said too much or too little, and I must say I need an explanation of his words. You say you don’t like this voyage. Now, why not?”

“I was hired, sir, on what we call sealed orders, to sail this ship wherever that gentleman directed me,” said the captain. “So far so good. But now I find that every common sailor on board knows more than I do. I don’t call that fair, now, do you?”
“No,” said Dr. Livesey, “I don’t.”

“Next,” said the captain, “I learn we’re going after treasure—hear it from my own crew, mind you. Now, treasure is dangerous work; I don’t like treasure voyages under any circumstances, and I especially don’t like them when they’re secret and when (begging your pardon, Mr. Trelawney) the secret has been told to the parrot.”
“Silver’s parrot?” asked the squire.

“It’s a figure of speech,” said the captain. “Blabbed, I mean. It’s my belief that neither of you gentlemen knows what you’re getting into, but I’ll tell you how I see it—it’s a matter of life or death, and a close call at that.”

“That’s all clear enough, and true enough, I dare say,” replied Dr. Livesey. “We accept the risk, but we’re not as ignorant as you think us. Next, you say you don’t like the crew. Aren’t they good seamen?”
“I don’t like them, sir,” returned Captain Smollett. “And I think I should have had the choosing of my own crew, if it comes to that.”
“Perhaps you should have,” replied the doctor. “My friend should perhaps have brought you in from the start, but the slight, if there was one, was unintentional. And you don’t like Mr. Arrow?”
“I don’t, sir. I believe he’s a capable seaman, but he’s too free with the crew to make a good officer. A mate should keep himself apart—he shouldn’t be drinking with the common hands!”
“Do you mean he drinks?” cried the squire.
“No, sir,” replied the captain, “only that he’s too familiar with them.”
“Very well, what’s the sum of it all, captain?” asked the doctor. “Tell us what you want.”
“Well, gentlemen, are you truly set on going through with this voyage?”
“Like iron,” answered the squire.

“Very good,” said the captain. “Then, since you’ve heard me out very patiently while I said things I couldn’t prove, hear me a few words more. They are putting the powder and the arms in the fore hold. Now, you have a good space under the cabin—why not put them there? That’s my first point. Then, you are bringing four of your own people with you, and I’m told some of them are to be berthed forward. Why not give them the berths here beside the cabin? That’s my second point.”
“Anything else?” asked Mr. Trelawney.
“One more thing,” said the captain. “There’s already been far too much loose talk.”
“Far too much,” agreed the doctor.

“I’ll tell you what I’ve heard myself,” continued Captain Smollett: “that you have a map of an island, that there are crosses on the map to mark where treasure is buried, and that the island lies—” And then he named the latitude and longitude exactly.
“I never told that,” cried the squire, “to a living soul!”
“The hands know it, sir,” returned the captain.
“Livesey, that must have been you or Hawkins,” cried the squire.

“It doesn’t much matter who it was,” replied the doctor. And I could see that neither he nor the captain paid much attention to Mr. Trelawney’s protests. Neither did I, to be honest—he was such a careless talker. Yet in this case I believe he was genuinely right, and that no one had actually given away the location of the island.
“Well, gentlemen,” continued the captain, “I don’t know who has this map, but I insist it be kept secret even from me and Mr. Arrow. Otherwise I would have to ask you to let me resign my command.”

“I see,” said the doctor. “You want us to keep this matter quiet and to fortify the stern part of the ship, manned by my friend’s own people, and stocked with all the arms and powder on board. In other words, you’re afraid of a mutiny.”

“Sir,” said Captain Smollett, “with no intention of taking offence, I deny your right to put words into my mouth. No captain would be justified in going to sea at all if he had firm enough grounds to say that outright. As for Mr. Arrow, I believe him to be thoroughly honest; some of the men are the same; all of them may be, for all I know. But I am responsible for the safety of this ship and the life of every man jack aboard her. I can see things going, in my view, not quite right. And so I ask you to take certain precautions, or let me step down from my command. And that’s all.”

“Captain Smollett,” began the doctor with a smile, “did you ever hear the fable of the mountain and the mouse? You’ll forgive me for saying so, but you remind me of it. When you came in here, I’d stake my reputation that you meant a good deal more than this.”
“Doctor,” said the captain, “you’re sharp. When I came in here I intended to get myself discharged. I never thought Mr. Trelawney would hear me out for a moment.”
“Nor would I,” cried the squire. “If Livesey hadn’t been here I’d have sent you packing. As it is, I’ve listened to you. I’ll do as you ask, but I think the worse of you for it.”
“That’s your right, sir,” said the captain. “You’ll find I do my duty.”
And with that he took his leave.
“Trelawney,” said the doctor, “contrary to all my expectations, I believe you’ve managed to get two honest men on board with you—that man and John Silver.”
“Silver, if you like,” cried the squire; “but as for that insufferable humbug, I declare I find his conduct unmanly, unsailorly, and downright un-English.”
“Well,” said the doctor, “we shall see.”
When we came back on deck, the men had already begun moving out the arms and powder, calling out cheerfully as they worked, while the captain and Mr. Arrow stood by supervising.

The new arrangement suited me well enough. The whole schooner had been overhauled; six berths had been fitted out in the stern from what had been the after-part of the main hold, and this cluster of cabins was connected to the galley and forecastle only by a sparred passage along the port side. Originally the captain, Mr. Arrow, Hunter, Joyce, the doctor, and the squire were to occupy these six berths. Now Redruth and I were to get two of them, while Mr. Arrow and the captain were to sleep on deck in the companion, which had been widened on either side until you could almost call it a round-house. It was still quite low, of course, but there was room enough to swing two hammocks, and even the mate seemed pleased with the arrangement. Perhaps he too had had his doubts about the crew—but that is only a guess, for as you shall hear, we did not long benefit from his opinion.
We were all hard at work shifting the powder and rearranging the berths when the last few men, with Long John among them, came off to the ship in a shore-boat.
The cook clambered up the ship’s side as nimbly as a monkey, and as soon as he saw what was going on, “So ho, mates!” says he. “What’s all this?”
“We’re shifting the powder, Jack,” answered one of the men.
“Why, by the powers,” cried Long John, “if we do that, we’ll miss the morning tide!”
“My orders!” said the captain sharply. “You may go below, my man. The hands will want their supper.”
“Aye, aye, sir,” answered the cook, and touching his forelock, he disappeared at once toward his galley.
“That’s a good man, captain,” said the doctor.

“Very likely, sir,” replied Captain Smollett. “Easy with that, men—easy,” he called out to the fellows shifting the powder; and then, suddenly noticing me examining the swivel gun we carried amidships, a long brass nine-pounder, “Here, you, ship’s boy,” he cried, “out of that! Off with you to the cook and find some work to do.”
And as I hurried away I heard him say, quite clearly, to the doctor, “I’ll have no favourites on my ship.”
I can assure you I agreed completely with the squire’s view of things, and thoroughly despised the captain.

chapters.title: The Voyage
paragraphs: All that night we were in a great bustle getting things stowed in their places, and boatfuls of the squire’s friends—Mr. Blandly and the like—came off to wish him a good voyage and a safe return. I’d never had a night at the Admiral Benbow when I had half so much work; and I was dead on my feet when, a little before dawn, the boatswain sounded his pipe and the crew began to man the capstan bars. I might have been twice as weary and still wouldn’t have left the deck, it was all so new and interesting to me—the brief commands, the shrill note of the whistle, the men bustling to their places in the glimmer of the ship’s lanterns.
“Now, Barbecue, give us a song,” cried one voice.
“The old one,” cried another.
“Aye, aye, mates,” said Long John, who was standing by with his crutch under his arm, and at once broke into the air and words I knew so well:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest--”
And then the whole crew joined in the chorus:
“Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”
And at the third “Ho!” they drove the bars before them with a will.

Even in that exciting moment it carried me back to the old Admiral Benbow in an instant, and I seemed to hear the voice of the captain joining in the chorus. But soon the anchor was short up; soon it was hanging dripping at the bows; soon the sails began to draw, and the land and shipping slid by on either side; and before I could lie down to snatch an hour of sleep, the Hispaniola had begun her voyage to the Isle of Treasure.

I’m not going to describe that voyage in detail. It was fairly prosperous. The ship proved to be a good one, the crew were capable seamen, and the captain thoroughly understood his business. But before we reached Treasure Island, two or three things happened that need to be told.

Mr. Arrow, first of all, turned out even worse than the captain had feared. He had no authority over the men, and people did as they pleased with him. But that was by no means the worst of it, for after a day or two at sea he began to appear on deck with glazed eyes, red cheeks, a stuttering tongue, and other signs of drunkenness. Time after time he was ordered below in disgrace. Sometimes he fell and cut himself; sometimes he lay all day long in his little bunk beside the companionway; sometimes for a day or two he would be nearly sober and attend to his work at least passably.

In the meantime, we could never figure out where he got the drink. That was the ship’s mystery. Watch him as we might, we could do nothing to solve it; and when we asked him to his face, he would only laugh if he were drunk, and if he were sober deny solemnly that he ever touched anything but water.

He was not only useless as an officer and a bad influence among the men, but it was clear that at this rate he must soon kill himself outright, so nobody was much surprised, nor very sorry, when one dark night, with a heavy sea running, he disappeared entirely and was never seen again.
“Overboard!” said the captain. “Well, gentlemen, that saves the trouble of putting him in irons.”

But there we were, without a mate; and it was necessary, of course, to promote one of the men. The boatswain, Job Anderson, was the likeliest man aboard, and though he kept his old title, he served in a way as mate. Mr. Trelawney had followed the sea, and his knowledge made him very useful, for he often took a watch himself in easy weather. And the coxswain, Israel Hands, was a careful, wily, experienced old seaman who could be trusted in a pinch with almost anything.
He was a great confidant of Long John Silver, and so the mention of his name leads me to speak of our ship’s cook, Barbecue, as the men called him.

Aboard ship he carried his crutch by a lanyard around his neck, to keep both hands as free as possible. It was something to see him wedge the foot of the crutch against a bulkhead, and propped against it—yielding to every movement of the ship—get on with his cooking like someone safe ashore. Still more remarkable was it to see him cross the deck in the heaviest weather. He had a line or two rigged up to help him across the widest spaces—Long John’s earrings, they were called—and he would haul himself from one place to another, now using the crutch, now trailing it alongside by the lanyard, as quickly as another man could walk. Yet some of the men who had sailed with him before expressed their pity to see him so reduced.

“He’s no common man, Barbecue,” said the coxswain to me. “He had good schooling in his young days and can speak like a book when he’s of a mind to; and brave—a lion’s nothing alongside of Long John! I’ve seen him grapple four men and knock their heads together—him unarmed.”

All the crew respected and even obeyed him. He had a way of talking to each man and doing everyone some particular service. To me he was endlessly kind, and always glad to see me in the galley, which he kept as clean as a new pin, the dishes hanging up burnished, and his parrot in a cage in one corner.

“Come in, Hawkins,” he would say; “come and have a yarn with John. Nobody more welcome than yourself, my son. Sit you down and hear the news. Here’s Cap’n Flint—I calls my parrot Cap’n Flint, after the famous buccaneer—here’s Cap’n Flint predicting success to our v’yage. Wasn’t you, Cap’n?”
And the parrot would say, with great rapidity, “Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!” till you wondered it wasn’t out of breath, or till John threw his handkerchief over the cage.

“Now, that bird,” he would say, “is maybe two hundred years old, Hawkins—they live forever mostly; and if anybody’s seen more wickedness, it must be the devil himself. She’s sailed with England, the great Cap’n England, the pirate. She’s been at Madagascar, and at Malabar, and Surinam, and Providence, and Portobello. She was there for the fishing up of the wrecked plate ships. That’s where she learned ‘Pieces of eight,’ and small wonder—three hundred and fifty thousand of ’em, Hawkins! She was at the boarding of the Viceroy of the Indies out of Goa, she was; and to look at her you’d think she was a baby. But you’ve smelled powder—haven’t you, Cap’n?”
“Stand by to go about,” the parrot would scream.

“Ah, she’s a handsome creature, she is,” the cook would say, and give her sugar from his pocket, and then the bird would peck at the bars and swear straight on, past all belief for wickedness. “There,” John would add, “you can’t touch pitch and not be dirtied, lad. Here’s this poor old innocent bird of mine swearing blue fire, and none the wiser—you may lay to that. She’d swear the same, in a manner of speaking, before a chaplain.” And John would touch his forelock with a solemn air he had that made me think he was the best of men.

In the meantime, the squire and Captain Smollett were still on pretty distant terms with one another. The squire made no bones about it; he despised the captain. The captain, for his part, never spoke unless he was spoken to, and then sharp and short and dry, with not a word wasted. He admitted, when pressed into a corner, that he seemed to have been wrong about the crew—that some of them were as brisk as he could wish, and all had behaved fairly well. As for the ship, he had taken a genuine liking to her. “She’ll lie a point nearer the wind than a man has any right to expect of his own wedded wife, sir. But,” he would add, “all I say is, we’re not home again, and I don’t like the cruise.”
The squire, at this, would turn away and march up and down the deck, chin in air.
“A trifle more of that man,” he would say, “and I shall explode.”

We had some heavy weather, which only proved the qualities of the Hispaniola. Every man on board seemed perfectly content, and they would have had to be hard to please if they hadn’t been, for it’s my belief there was never a ship’s company so spoiled since Noah put to sea. Double grog was handed out on the slightest excuse; there was duff on odd days—if the squire heard it was any man’s birthday, for instance—and always a barrel of apples standing open in the waist for anyone to help himself.
“Never knew good to come of it yet,” the captain said to Dr. Livesey. “Spoil forecastle hands and you make devils. That’s my belief.”
But good did come of the apple barrel, as you shall hear, for if it had not been for that, we would have had no note of warning and might all have perished by the hand of treachery.
This is how it came about.

We had run up the trades to get the wind of the island we were after—I am not allowed to be more specific—and now we were running down for it with a sharp lookout day and night. It was about the last day of our outward voyage by the most generous reckoning; sometime that night, or at latest before noon the next day, we should sight Treasure Island. We were heading S.S.W. and had a steady breeze abeam and a quiet sea. The Hispaniola rolled steadily, dipping her bowsprit now and then with a whiff of spray. Everything was drawing aloft and alow; everyone was in the highest spirits because we were now so near the end of the first part of our adventure.

Now, just after sundown, when all my work was done and I was on my way to my berth, it occurred to me that I should like an apple. I ran on deck. The watch was all forward looking out for the island. The man at the helm was watching the luff of the sail and whistling softly to himself, and that was the only sound apart from the swish of the sea against the bows and around the sides of the ship.

I climbed bodily into the apple barrel and found there were scarce any apples left; but sitting down there in the dark, between the sound of the water and the rocking motion of the ship, I had either fallen asleep or was on the point of doing so when a heavy man sat down with rather a crash close by. The barrel shook as he leaned his shoulders against it, and I was just about to jump up when the man began to speak. It was Silver’s voice, and before I had heard a dozen words, I would not have shown myself for all the world, but lay there trembling and listening in the grip of fear and curiosity—for from those dozen words I understood that the lives of all the honest men aboard depended on me alone.

chapters.title: What I Heard in the Apple-Barrel
paragraphs: "No, not I," said Silver. "Flint was captain; I was quartermaster, on account of my timber leg. The same broadside that cost me my leg took old Pew's eyesight. The surgeon that amputated me was a fine man—proper college education, Latin by the bucketful, and all the rest—but he was hanged like a dog and left to dry in the sun like the others at Corso Castle. Those were Roberts' men, and it came from their habit of changing their ships' names—ROYAL FORTUNE and the like. Now, what a ship is christened, that's what she should stay, I say. So it was with the CASSANDRA, which brought us all safely home from Malabar after England captured the Viceroy of the Indies; so it was with the old WALRUS, Flint's old ship, which I've seen running red with blood and ready to sink under the weight of gold."
"Ah!" cried another voice, clearly the youngest hand on board, and full of admiration. "He was the best of the lot, was Flint!"

"Davis was a man too, by all accounts," said Silver. "I never sailed with him; first it was England, then Flint, that's my story; and now here on my own account, in a manner of speaking. I put away nine hundred safe from England, and two thousand after Flint. That's not bad for a man before the mast—all safe in the bank. It isn't earning that does it now, it's saving, you can count on that. Where are all England's men now? I couldn't say. Where are Flint's? Why, most of them are aboard this ship, glad enough to get their pudding—some of them were begging before that. Old Pew, who had lost his sight, and might have known better, spent twelve hundred pounds in a year, like a lord in Parliament. Where is he now? Well, he's dead and buried; but for two years before that, shiver my timbers, the man was starving! He begged, and he stole, and he cut throats, and starved all the same, by thunder!"
"Well, it doesn't seem worth much, after all," said the young seaman.

"It isn't worth much for fools, you can count on that—not this, nor anything else," cried Silver. "But listen here: you're young, you are, but you're sharp as a pin. I saw that the moment I set eyes on you, and I'll talk to you straight."

You can imagine how I felt when I heard this vile old rogue speaking to another in the very same words of flattery he had used on me. I think, if I had been able, I would have killed him right there through the barrel. Meanwhile, he went on talking, with no idea he was being overheard.

"Here's the thing about gentlemen of fortune. They live rough, and they risk the gallows, but they eat and drink like fighting-cocks, and when a voyage is done, why, it's hundreds of pounds instead of hundreds of pennies in their pockets. Now, most of them blow it all on rum and a good spree, then go back to sea in their shirtsleeves. But that's not the course I sail. I put it all away, some here, some there, and not too much in any one place, to avoid suspicion. I'm fifty, mark you; once back from this cruise, I set myself up as a gentleman for real. High time too, you'll say. Ah, but I've lived well in the meantime, never denied myself anything my heart desired, and slept soft and eaten fine all my days except when at sea. And where did I start? Before the mast, same as you!"
"Well," said the other, "but all the other money's gone now, isn't it? You can't show your face in Bristol after this."
"Why, where do you suppose it was?" asked Silver with a sneer.
"In Bristol, in banks and such places," answered his companion.

"It was," said the cook; "it was there when we weighed anchor. But my old wife has it all by now. And the Spy-glass is sold—lease and goodwill and fittings—and the old girl's off to meet me. I'd tell you where, for I trust you, but it would stir up jealousy among the crew."
"And can you trust your wife?" asked the other.

"Gentlemen of fortune," returned the cook, "generally trust very little among themselves, and rightly so, you can count on it. But I have a way with me, I do. When a mate of mine slips up—one who knows me, I mean—he won't be in this world anymore to trouble old John. There were some who feared Pew, and some who feared Flint; but Flint himself was afraid of me. Afraid he was, and proud of it. They were the roughest crew afloat, was Flint's; the devil himself would have been scared to sail with them. Well now, I tell you, I'm not a boastful man, and you've seen yourself how easy I keep company, but when I was quartermaster, LAMBS wasn't the word for Flint's old buccaneers. Ah, you may feel safe in old John's ship."
"Well, I'll tell you now," replied the lad, "I didn't half like the job until I had this talk with you, John; but here's my hand on it now."
"And a brave lad you are, and a sharp one too," answered Silver, shaking hands so heartily that the whole barrel shook, "and a finer figurehead for a gentleman of fortune I never set eyes on."

By this time I had begun to understand the meaning of their words. By a "gentleman of fortune" they plainly meant nothing more nor less than a common pirate, and the little scene I had overheard was the final act in the corruption of one of the honest hands—perhaps the last honest man left aboard. But on this point I was soon to be reassured, for Silver gave a low whistle and a third man came strolling up to join the group.
"Dick's in," said Silver.

"Oh, I always knew Dick would come in," returned the voice of the coxswain, Israel Hands. "He's no fool, is Dick." And he shifted his chew of tobacco and spat. "But listen here," he went on, "here's what I want to know, Barbecue: how long are we going to keep sailing back and forth like some blessed supply boat? I've had just about enough of Captain Smollett; he's pushed me around long enough, blast it! I want to get into that cabin, I do. I want their pickles and wine, and all the rest."

"Israel," said Silver, "your head was never much use, and still isn't. But you can hear well enough, I expect; your ears are certainly big enough. Now, here's what I say: you'll sleep forward, and you'll live hard, and you'll speak quiet, and you'll stay sober until I give the word; and you can count on that, my lad."
"Well, I'm not arguing, am I?" growled the coxswain. "What I'm asking is, when? That's what I want to know."

"When! By thunder!" cried Silver. "Well now, if you want to know, I'll tell you when. The last possible moment I can manage—that's when. Here we have a first-rate seaman, Captain Smollett, sailing this blessed ship for us. Here's the squire and doctor with a map and such—I don't know where the treasure is, do I? No more do you, you'll say. Well then, I mean for this squire and doctor to find the goods and help us get them aboard, by thunder. Then we'll see. If I were sure of all of you, sons of double Dutchmen, I'd have Captain Smollett navigate us halfway home before I made my move."
"Why, we're all seamen aboard here, I should think," said young Dick.

"We're all forecastle hands, you mean," snapped Silver. "We can steer a course, but who's to set one? That's where all you gentlemen come to grief, every time. If I had my way, I'd have Captain Smollett work us back into the trade winds at least; then we'd have no blundering navigation and a spoonful of water a day. But I know your sort. I'll be done with them at the island, as soon as the treasure's on board, and it's a pity too. But you're never happy until you're drunk. Split my sides, it turns my stomach to sail with the likes of you!"
"Easy there, Long John," cried Israel. "Who's crossing you?"

"Why, how many fine ships do you think I've seen captured and seized? And how many bright lads left hanging at Execution Dock?" cried Silver. "And all from this same hurry and hurry and hurry. Do you hear me? I've seen a thing or two at sea, I have. If you would only hold your course and give yourself a little margin to windward, you'd be riding in carriages, you would. But not you lot! I know you. You'll have your mouthful of rum tomorrow and go hang."

"Everyone knows you're a kind of a preacher, John; but there's others who could handle a ship as well as you," said Israel. "They liked a bit of fun, they did. They weren't so prim and proper, not by a long shot, but took their pleasure, like jolly companions all."
"So?" says Silver. "Well, and where are they now? Pew was that sort, and he died a beggar. Flint was, and he died of rum in Savannah. Ah, they were a sweet crew indeed! Only, where are they?"
"But," asked Dick, "when we do move against them, what are we to do with them anyway?"

"Now there's the man for me!" cried the cook approvingly. "That's what I call getting down to business. Well, what would you think? Put them ashore as castaways? That would have been England's way. Or cut them down like so much meat? That would have been Flint's way, or Billy Bones's."
"Billy was the man for that," said Israel. "'Dead men don't bite,' says he. Well, he's dead himself now; he knows the whole story firsthand; and if ever a tough hand came to port, it was Billy."

"Right you are," said Silver; "rough and ready. But mark me here, I'm an easy man—quite the gentleman, you'll say; but this time it's serious. Duty is duty, mates. I give my vote—death. When I'm in Parliament and riding in my coach, I don't want any of these sea-lawyers coming back to the cabin, turning up uninvited like the devil at prayers. Wait is what I say; but when the time comes, why, let it rip!"
"John," cries the coxswain, "you're a man!"

"You'll say so, Israel, when you see," said Silver. "Only one thing I claim for myself—I claim Trelawney. I'll wring his calf's head off his body with these hands, Dick!" he added, breaking off. "Just hop up like a good lad and get me an apple, to wet my throat."

You can imagine the terror I was in! I would have leaped out and run for it if I had found the strength, but my limbs and heart alike failed me. I heard Dick begin to get up, and then someone seemed to stop him, and the voice of Hands called out, "Oh, forget that! Don't go drinking from that bilge, John. Let's have a go of the rum instead."
"Dick," said Silver, "I trust you. I've got a gauge on the keg, mind. Here's the key; you fill a cup and bring it up."
Terrified as I was, I could not help thinking to myself that this must have been how Mr. Arrow had gotten the strong drink that had done for him.

Dick was gone only a short while, and during his absence Israel spoke quietly into the cook's ear. I caught only a word or two, and yet I gathered some important news, for besides other scraps that pointed the same way, this whole sentence came through clearly: "Not another man of them'll join." So there were still loyal men on board.

When Dick returned, the three men took the cup in turn and drank—one with "To luck," another with "Here's to old Flint," and Silver himself saying in a kind of singsong, "Here's to ourselves, and hold your course, plenty of prizes and plenty of pudding."

Just then a kind of brightness fell on me inside the barrel, and looking up, I found that the moon had risen and was silvering the mizzen-top and shining white on the luff of the foresail; and almost at the same moment the voice of the lookout rang out from above: "Land ho!"

chapters.title: Council of War
paragraphs: There was a sudden stampede of feet across the deck. I could hear people scrambling up from the cabin and the forecastle, and in an instant I slipped out of my barrel, ducked behind the foresail, made a wide loop toward the stern, and came out on the open deck just in time to join Hunter and Dr. Livesey in the rush for the windward bow.

All hands were already crowding the rail. A wall of fog had lifted almost at the same moment the moon appeared. Away to the south-west we could see two low hills, roughly a couple of miles apart, and rising behind one of them a third, taller hill whose peak was still swallowed in the fog. All three looked sharp and cone-shaped.

I took this in as though half-dreaming, for I hadn't yet recovered from the terror of those minutes in the barrel. Then I heard Captain Smollett's voice snapping out orders. The Hispaniola was brought a couple of points closer to the wind, and she settled onto a course that would clear the island on the east.
"And now, men," said the captain, once all the sails were trimmed, "has any one of you ever seen that land ahead?"
"I have, sir," said Silver. "I watered there once on a trading vessel I was cook on."
"The anchorage is on the south side, behind an islet, I believe?" the captain asked.

"Yes, sir; Skeleton Island they call it. It was a big place for pirates once, and a crewman we had aboard knew all their names for it. That hill to the north they call the Foremast Hill; there are three hills in a row running southward — fore, main, and mizzen, sir. But the main one — that's the big one with the cloud on it — they usually call the Spy-glass, because of the lookout they kept there when they were at anchor careening their ships, sir, begging your pardon."
"I have a chart here," said Captain Smollett. "See if that's the place."

Long John's eyes lit up as he took the chart, but from the fresh look of the paper I knew he was in for a disappointment. This wasn't the map we'd found in Billy Bones's chest — it was an accurate copy, complete in every detail: names, heights, soundings — but with the single exception that the red crosses and the handwritten notes were missing. However sharp his frustration must have been, Silver had the self-control to keep it hidden.

"Yes, sir," said he, "this is the spot, right enough, and very neatly drawn out. I wonder who did it? The pirates were too ignorant, I'd reckon. Aye, here it is: 'Capt. Kidd's Anchorage' — that's exactly the name my shipmate used for it. There's a strong current running along the south, and then away northward up the west coast. You were right, sir," says he, "to haul your wind and keep to the windward of the island. That is, if your intention was to enter and careen — and there's no better place for it in these waters."
"Thank you, my man," said Captain Smollett. "I'll ask you later on to give us a hand. You may go."

I was surprised at how casually John admitted his knowledge of the island, and I'll confess I was half frightened when I saw him moving toward me. He didn't know, of course, that I had overheard his plotting from inside the apple barrel, and yet by this point I had developed such a horror of his cruelty, his treachery, and his power that I could barely hide a shudder when he laid his hand on my arm.

"Ah," says he, "this is a lovely spot, this island — a lovely spot for a lad to go ashore on. You'll swim, and climb trees, and hunt goats, you will; and you'll scramble over those hills as nimbly as a goat yourself. Why, it makes me feel young again. I nearly forgot about my timber leg. It's a fine thing to be young with ten toes, and you can count on that. When you want to go exploring, you just ask old John, and he'll pack a snack for you to take along."
And clapping me on the shoulder in the friendliest way, he hobbled off toward the bow and went below.

Captain Smollett, the squire, and Dr. Livesey were talking together on the quarterdeck, and anxious as I was to tell them everything, I didn't dare interrupt them openly. While I was still trying to think of a plausible excuse, Dr. Livesey called me over. He said he had left his pipe below and needed me to fetch it; but as soon as I was close enough to speak without being overheard, I came straight out with it: "Doctor, let me speak. Get the captain and squire down to the cabin, and then make some excuse to send for me. I have terrible news."
The doctor's expression shifted for just a moment, but the next instant he had himself under control.
"Thank you, Jim," he said, quite loudly, "that was all I wanted to know" — as though he had simply asked me a question.

With that he turned on his heel and rejoined the other two. They talked together briefly, and though none of them flinched, raised his voice, or so much as whistled, it was plain that Dr. Livesey had passed on my message — for the next thing I heard was the captain giving an order to Job Anderson, and all hands were piped on deck.

"Men," said Captain Smollett, "I have a word to say to you. The land we've just sighted is the place we've been sailing for. Mr. Trelawney, being the generous gentleman he is, as we all know, has just had a brief word with me, and since I was able to tell him that every man aboard had done his duty, aloft and below, as well as I've ever seen it done, he and I and the doctor are going below to the cabin to drink your health and good fortune, and you'll have grog served out so you can drink ours. I call that handsome. And if you agree with me, give a good sea-cheer for the gentleman who's doing it."
The cheer followed — that was a given; but it rang out so full and hearty that I could scarcely believe these same men were plotting to have us killed.
"One more cheer for Cap'n Smollett," cried Long John when the first had died down.
And this too was given with gusto.
After that, the three gentlemen went below, and not long after, word was sent forward that Jim Hawkins was wanted in the cabin.

I found all three of them sitting around the table, a bottle of Spanish wine and some raisins set out before them, and the doctor smoking away with his wig on his lap — which I knew was a sign that he was unsettled. The stern window stood open, it being a warm night, and you could see the moonlight shimmering on the ship's wake.
"Now, Hawkins," said the squire, "you have something to tell us. Speak up."

I did as I was told, and as briefly as I could, I laid out every detail of Silver's conversation. Nobody interrupted me until I'd finished, and none of the three made so much as a movement throughout — they kept their eyes fixed on my face from start to finish.
"Jim," said Dr. Livesey, "take a seat."

They had me sit down at the table beside them, poured me a glass of wine, filled my hands with raisins, and all three of them, one after another, each with a bow, drank to my health and thanked me for my luck and courage.
"Now, captain," said the squire, "you were right, and I was wrong. I admit I was a fool, and I await your orders."

"No more a fool than I, sir," replied the captain. "I've never known a crew that meant to mutiny without showing some sign of it beforehand — plain enough for any man with eyes to see the danger and act accordingly. But this crew," he added, "has me stumped."
"Captain," said the doctor, "if you'll allow me — that's Silver's doing. A most remarkable man."

"He'd look remarkably well dangling from a yardarm, sir," returned the captain. "But this is talk; it doesn't get us anywhere. I can see three or four points we need to address, and with Mr. Trelawney's permission, I'll lay them out."
"You are the captain. It is for you to speak," said Mr. Trelawney grandly.

"First point," began Mr. Smollett. "We must press on, because turning back isn't an option. If I gave the order to come about, they'd rise against us immediately. Second point, we have some time — at least until the treasure is found. Third point, there are loyal hands among the crew. Now, sir, it will come to a fight sooner or later, and what I propose is to seize the moment and strike on a day when they least expect it. We can count on your own household servants, Mr. Trelawney, can we not?"
"As surely as on myself," declared the squire.
"Three," counted the captain; "and we ourselves make seven, counting Hawkins here. Now, what about the honest hands in the crew?"
"Most likely Trelawney's own men," said the doctor — "those he had chosen for himself before he fell in with Silver."
"No," replied the squire. "Hands was one of mine."
"I did think I could have trusted Hands," added the captain.
"And to think they're all Englishmen!" burst out the squire. "Sir, I could find it in my heart to blow the ship to pieces."

"Well, gentlemen," said the captain, "the best I can offer isn't much. We must hold steady, if you please, and keep a sharp lookout. I know it's hard on a man's nerves. It would feel better to come to blows. But there's no choice until we know who we can count on. Hold tight and wait for our chance — that's my view."
"Jim here," said the doctor, "can help us more than anyone. The men don't guard themselves around him, and Jim notices things."
"Hawkins, I have enormous faith in you," added the squire.

I felt a creeping despair at this, for I felt utterly powerless; and yet, by a strange twist of fate, it was through me that safety eventually came. In the meantime, for all our talk, there were only seven out of twenty-six on whom we knew we could rely; and of those seven, one was a boy — so the grown men on our side numbered six against their nineteen.

chapters.title: How I Began My Shore Adventure
paragraphs: The look of the island had completely changed by the time I came on deck the next morning. The breeze had died away entirely, but we had made good progress during the night and now lay becalmed about half a mile southeast of the low eastern coast. Grey-colored woods covered most of the surface. The even tint was broken up by streaks of yellow sand in the lower lands and by many tall pines that overtopped the other trees—some standing alone, some in clumps—but the overall coloring was uniform and sad. The hills rose above the vegetation in spires of bare rock. All were strangely shaped, and the Spy-glass, which was three or four hundred feet taller than anything else on the island, was also the strangest in shape, rising sheer from almost every side and then suddenly cut off at the top like a pedestal made to hold a statue.

The Hispaniola was rolling her scuppers under in the ocean swell. The booms were tugging at the blocks, the rudder was banging back and forth, and the whole ship creaked, groaned, and jumped like a factory. I had to cling tight to the backstay, and the world spun dizzily before my eyes. I was a decent enough sailor when the ship was moving, but standing still and being rolled around like a bottle was something I never learned to handle without feeling sick—especially in the morning, on an empty stomach.

Perhaps it was that, or perhaps it was the look of the island itself, with its grey, melancholy woods, its wild stone spires, and the surf we could both see and hear foaming and thundering on the steep beach. Even though the sun shone bright and hot, and the shore birds were fishing and calling all around us, and you would have thought anyone would be glad to reach land after so long at sea, my heart sank, as the saying goes, into my boots. From the first glance onward, I hated the very thought of Treasure Island.

We had a dreary morning's work ahead of us, because there was no wind, and the boats had to be lowered and manned, and the ship warped three or four miles around the corner of the island and up the narrow passage to the harbor behind Skeleton Island. I volunteered for one of the boats, where I had no real business being. The heat was sweltering, and the men grumbled fiercely over their work. Anderson was in command of my boat, and instead of keeping the crew in order, he grumbled as loudly as the worst of them.
"Well," he said with a curse, "it's not forever."
I thought that was a very bad sign, because up to that day the men had gone briskly and willingly about their work. But the mere sight of the island had loosened the cords of discipline.

All the way in, Long John stood by the helmsman and conned the ship. He knew the passage like the palm of his hand, and though the man taking soundings kept finding more water everywhere than the chart showed, John never hesitated once.
"There's a strong scour with the ebb," he said, "and this passage has been dug out, you might say, with a spade."

We anchored just where the chart marked the anchor, about a third of a mile from each shore—the mainland on one side and Skeleton Island on the other. The bottom was clean sand. The splash of our anchor sent clouds of birds wheeling and crying over the woods, but in less than a minute they had settled again and all was silent once more.

The place was entirely land-locked, buried in woods, with the trees coming right down to the high-water mark. The shores were mostly flat, and the hilltops stood around at a distance in a kind of amphitheater, one here, one there. Two little rivers, or rather two swamps, drained into this pond, as you might call it, and the foliage around that part of the shore had a kind of poisonous brightness. From the ship we could see nothing of the house or stockade, since they were completely buried among trees; and if it hadn't been for the chart on the companion, we might have thought we were the first ever to anchor there since the island rose out of the sea.

There was not a breath of air moving, nor any sound except the surf booming half a mile away along the beaches and against the outer rocks. A peculiar stagnant smell hung over the anchorage—a smell of sodden leaves and rotting tree trunks. I noticed the doctor sniffing and sniffing, like someone tasting a bad egg.
"I don't know about treasure," he said, "but I'll stake my wig there's fever here."

If the men's behavior had been alarming in the boat, it became truly threatening once they were back on board. They lay around the deck growling together in their talk. The slightest order was met with a black look and obeyed grudgingly and carelessly. Even the honest hands must have caught the infection, because there wasn't one man aboard who would correct another. Mutiny, plainly, hung over us like a thundercloud.

And we of the cabin party weren't the only ones who saw the danger. Long John was hard at work going from group to group, pouring out good advice, and as for setting an example no man could have shown a better one. He fairly outdid himself in willingness and politeness; he was all smiles to everyone. If an order came down, John was on his crutch in an instant with the cheeriest "Aye, aye, sir!" in the world; and when there was nothing else to do, he kept up one song after another, as if to cover the discontent of the rest.
Of all the gloomy features of that gloomy afternoon, this obvious anxiety on Long John's part seemed the worst.
We held a council in the cabin.

"Sir," said the captain, "if I risk another order, the whole ship will come down on us in a heartbeat. You see, sir, here's how it stands. I get a rough answer, don't I? Well, if I speak back, pikes will be out in two shakes; if I don't, Silver will see there's something behind it, and the game's up. Now, we have only one man to rely on."
"And who is that?" asked the squire.

"Silver, sir," answered the captain. "He's as eager as you and I to smooth things over. This is just a quarrel; he'd soon talk them out of it if he had the chance, and what I propose is to give him that chance. Let's allow the men an afternoon ashore. If they all go, then we'll fight for the ship. If none of them go, well then, we hold the cabin, and God defend the right. If some go, mark my words, sir, Silver will bring them back aboard as mild as lambs."

It was decided that way. Loaded pistols were handed out to all the trustworthy men. Hunter, Joyce, and Redruth were let in on the plan, and they received the news with less surprise and better spirits than we had expected. Then the captain went on deck and addressed the crew.

"My lads," he said, "it's been a hot day, and we're all tired and out of sorts. A turn ashore will hurt nobody—the boats are still in the water; you can take the gigs, and as many as please may go ashore for the afternoon. I'll fire a gun half an hour before sundown."

I believe the silly fellows must have thought they would trip over treasure as soon as they landed, because they all came out of their sulks in a moment and gave a cheer that woke the echo on a faraway hill and sent the birds flying and squalling around the anchorage once more.

The captain was too smart to be in the way. He whipped out of sight in a moment, leaving Silver to organize the shore party, and I think it was just as well he did. If he had stayed on deck, he could no longer have pretended not to understand the situation. It was as plain as day. Silver was the captain, and a mighty rebellious crew he had. The honest hands—and I was soon to see proof that there were such men on board—must have been very stupid fellows. Or rather, I suppose the truth was that all hands had been infected by the example of the ringleaders—some more, some less—and a few, being decent men at heart, could neither be led nor driven any further. It is one thing to loaf and slack off, and quite another to seize a ship and murder a number of innocent men.
At last, however, the party was made up. Six fellows were to stay on board, and the remaining thirteen, including Silver, began to climb into the boats.

That was when the first of the mad ideas came into my head—the ones that did so much to save our lives. If Silver was leaving six men aboard, it was plain our party couldn't take and fight the ship; and since only six were left, it was equally plain that the cabin party had no present need of my help. It suddenly occurred to me to go ashore. In a flash I had slipped over the side and curled up in the bow of the nearest boat, and almost at the same moment she pushed off.

No one noticed me, except the bow oar, who said, "Is that you, Jim? Keep your head down." But Silver, from the other boat, glanced over sharply and called out to ask if that was me; and from that moment I began to regret what I had done.

The crews raced for the beach, but the boat I was in, having a head start and being both lighter and better manned, shot far ahead of her partner. The bow struck among the shore-side trees, and I caught a branch and swung myself out and plunged into the nearest thicket while Silver and the rest were still a hundred yards behind.
"Jim, Jim!" I heard him shouting.
But you may suppose I paid no attention. Jumping, ducking, and crashing through, I ran straight ahead until I could run no farther.

chapters.title: The First Blow
paragraphs: I was so pleased at having given Long John the slip that I began to enjoy myself and look around with some interest at the strange land I was in.

I had crossed a marshy stretch full of willows, bulrushes, and odd, outlandish swamp trees, and I had now come out on the edge of an open piece of rolling, sandy country about a mile long, dotted with a few pines and a great number of contorted trees, not unlike oaks in their growth but pale in the foliage, like willows. On the far side of the open stood one of the hills, with two quaint, craggy peaks shining vividly in the sun.

For the first time I felt the joy of exploration. The island was uninhabited; I had left my shipmates behind, and nothing lived in front of me but dumb animals and birds. I wandered here and there among the trees. Here and there were flowering plants I didn't know; here and there I saw snakes, and one raised his head from a ledge of rock and hissed at me with a noise not unlike a spinning top. Little did I suspect that he was a deadly enemy and that the noise was the famous rattle.

Then I came to a long thicket of those oak-like trees—live oaks, or evergreen oaks, I heard afterward they should be called—which grew low along the sand like brambles, the boughs curiously twisted, the foliage compact, like thatch. The thicket stretched down from the top of one of the sandy knolls, spreading and growing taller as it went, until it reached the edge of the broad, reedy fen through which the nearest of the little rivers soaked its way into the anchorage. The marsh was steaming in the strong sun, and the outline of the Spy-glass trembled through the haze.

All at once a kind of commotion broke out among the bulrushes; a wild duck flew up with a quack, another followed, and soon over the whole surface of the marsh a great cloud of birds hung screaming and circling in the air. I judged at once that some of my shipmates must be drawing near along the edges of the fen. Nor was I wrong, for soon I heard the very distant, low tones of a human voice, which, as I kept listening, grew steadily louder and nearer.
This put me into great fear, and I crawled under the cover of the nearest live-oak and crouched there, listening, as silent as a mouse.

Another voice answered, and then the first voice, which I now recognized as Silver's, took up the talk again and ran on for a long while in a stream, only now and then interrupted by the other. By the sound of it they must have been talking earnestly, almost fiercely, but no distinct word reached my ears.

At last the speakers seemed to have paused, and perhaps to have sat down, because not only did they stop drawing any nearer, but the birds themselves began to grow quieter and to settle again into their places in the swamp.

And now I began to feel that I was neglecting my duty—that since I had been foolhardy enough to come ashore with these desperadoes, the least I could do was overhear them at their councils, and that my plain and obvious job was to draw as close as I could manage, under the helpful cover of the crouching trees.
I could tell the direction of the speakers pretty exactly, not only by the sound of their voices but by the behavior of the few birds that still hung in alarm above the heads of the intruders.

Crawling on all fours, I made steadily but slowly toward them, until at last, raising my head to an opening among the leaves, I could see clear down into a little green dell beside the marsh, closely set about with trees, where Long John Silver and another of the crew stood face to face in conversation.
The sun beat full upon them. Silver had thrown his hat beside him on the ground, and his great, smooth, blond face, all shining with heat, was lifted to the other man's in a kind of appeal.

"Mate," he was saying, "it's because I think gold dust of you—gold dust, and you can lay to that! If I hadn't taken to you like pitch, do you think I'd be here warning you? It's all up—you can't make nor mend; it's to save your neck that I'm speaking, and if one of the wild ones knew it, where would I be, Tom—now, tell me, where would I be?"

"Silver," said the other man—and I noticed he was not only red in the face, but spoke as hoarse as a crow, and his voice shook too, like a taut rope—"Silver," he said, "you're old, and you're honest, or you've got the name for it; and you've got money too, which lots of poor sailors haven't; and you're brave, or I'm mistaken. And will you tell me you'll let yourself be led away by that pack of swabs? Not you! As sure as God sees me, I'd sooner lose my hand. If I turn against my duty—"

And then all of a sudden he was interrupted by a noise. I had found one of the honest hands—well, here, at that same moment, came news of another. Far away out in the marsh there rose, all at once, a sound like a cry of anger, then another on the back of it, and then one horrid, long-drawn scream. The rocks of the Spy-glass re-echoed it a score of times; the whole troop of marsh-birds rose again, darkening the heavens, with a simultaneous whirr; and long after that death yell still rang in my brain, silence had reestablished its rule, and only the rustle of the redescending birds and the boom of the distant surf disturbed the languor of the afternoon.
Tom had leaped at the sound like a horse at the spur, but Silver had not blinked an eye. He stood where he was, resting lightly on his crutch, watching his companion like a snake about to strike.
"John!" said the sailor, stretching out his hand.
"Hands off!" cried Silver, leaping back a yard, as it seemed to me, with the speed and surety of a trained gymnast.
"Hands off, if you like, John Silver," said the other. "It's a black conscience that can make you afraid of me. But in heaven's name, tell me, what was that?"
"That?" said Silver, smiling away, but warier than ever, his eye a mere pinpoint in his big face but gleaming like a crumb of glass. "That? Oh, I reckon that'll be Alan."
And at that point Tom flashed out like a hero.

"Alan!" he cried. "Then God rest his soul for a true seaman! And as for you, John Silver, long you've been a mate of mine, but you're a mate of mine no more. If I die like a dog, I'll die doing my duty. You've killed Alan, have you? Kill me too, if you can. But I defy you."

And with that, this brave fellow turned his back directly on the cook and set off walking for the beach. But he was not destined to go far. With a cry, John seized the branch of a tree, whipped the crutch out of his armpit, and sent that crude missile hurtling through the air. It struck poor Tom, point foremost, with stunning force, right between the shoulders in the middle of his back. His hands flew up, he gave a sort of gasp, and fell.

Whether he was hurt much or little, no one could ever tell. Likely enough, judging from the sound, his back was broken on the spot. But he was given no time to recover. Silver, agile as a monkey even without his leg or crutch, was on top of him the next moment and had twice buried his knife to the hilt in that defenseless body. From my hiding place I could hear him pant aloud as he struck the blows.

I don't know exactly what it is to faint, but I do know that for the next little while the whole world swam away from before me in a whirling mist; Silver and the birds and the tall Spy-glass hilltop went round and round and topsy-turvy before my eyes, and all manner of bells were ringing and distant voices shouting in my ear.

When I came back to myself, the monster had pulled himself together, his crutch under his arm, his hat upon his head. Just in front of him Tom lay motionless on the turf; but the murderer paid him no attention, wiping his bloodstained knife meanwhile on a wisp of grass. Everything else was unchanged—the sun still shining mercilessly on the steaming marsh and the tall pinnacle of the mountain—and I could scarcely persuade myself that murder had actually been done and a human life cruelly cut short a moment ago before my eyes.

But now John put his hand into his pocket, brought out a whistle, and blew several modulated blasts on it that rang far across the heated air. I couldn't tell, of course, what the signal meant, but it instantly woke my fears. More men would be coming. I might be discovered. They had already killed two of the honest people; after Tom and Alan, might I not come next?

Instantly I began to extricate myself and crawl back, with what speed and silence I could manage, to the more open part of the wood. As I did so, I could hear hails passing back and forth between the old buccaneer and his comrades, and this sound of danger lent me wings. As soon as I was clear of the thicket, I ran as I had never run before, scarcely caring which direction I went, as long as it led me away from the murderers; and as I ran, fear grew and grew on me until it became a kind of frenzy.

Indeed, could anyone be more utterly lost than I was? When the gun fired, how was I to dare go down to the boats among those fiends, still steaming from their crime? Wouldn't the first of them who saw me wring my neck like a snipe's? Wouldn't my very absence be proof to them of my alarm, and therefore of my fatal knowledge? It was all over, I thought. Goodbye to the Hispaniola; goodbye to the squire, the doctor, and the captain! There was nothing left for me but death by starvation or death at the hands of the mutineers.

All this while, as I say, I was still running, and without paying any attention I had come near the foot of the little hill with the two peaks and had entered a part of the island where the live-oaks grew more widely apart and looked more like forest trees in their bearing and size. Mingled with them were a few scattered pines, some fifty feet high, some nearer seventy. The air also smelled fresher than down beside the marsh.
And here a fresh alarm brought me to a standstill, my heart thumping.

chapters.title: The Man of the Island
paragraphs: From the side of the hill, which was steep and stony here, a spout of gravel was knocked loose and fell rattling and bounding through the trees. My eyes turned instinctively in that direction, and I saw a figure leap with great speed behind the trunk of a pine. What it was—whether bear or man or monkey—I could not tell at all. It looked dark and shaggy; more than that I didn't know. But the terror of this new apparition brought me to a halt.

I was now, it seemed, cut off on both sides: behind me the murderers, in front of me this lurking nondescript. And immediately I began to prefer the dangers I knew to those I didn't. Silver himself seemed less terrible by comparison with this creature of the woods, and I turned on my heel, and, looking sharply behind me over my shoulder, began to retrace my steps in the direction of the boats.

Instantly the figure reappeared, and making a wide circuit, began to head me off. I was tired, anyway; but had I been as fresh as when I got up that morning, I could see it was useless for me to try to outrun such an opponent. From trunk to trunk the creature flitted like a deer, running on two legs like a man, but unlike any man I had ever seen, stooping almost double as it ran. Yet a man it was—I could no longer doubt it.

I began to recall what I had heard about cannibals. I was within a hair's breadth of calling for help. But the simple fact that he was a man, however wild, had somewhat reassured me, and my fear of Silver began to revive in proportion. So I stood still and looked around for some way to escape; and as I was thinking, the memory of my pistol flashed into my mind. As soon as I remembered I was not defenseless, courage glowed again in my heart, and I set my face resolutely toward this man of the island and walked briskly toward him.

By this time he was hidden behind another tree trunk; but he must have been watching me closely, because as soon as I began to move in his direction he reappeared and took a step to meet me. Then he hesitated, drew back, came forward again, and at last, to my surprise and confusion, threw himself on his knees and held out his clasped hands in supplication.
At that I stopped once more.
"Who are you?" I asked.
"Ben Gunn," he answered, and his voice sounded hoarse and awkward, like a rusty lock. "I'm poor Ben Gunn, I am; and I haven't spoke with a Christian these three years."

I could now see that he was a white man like me, and that his features were even pleasant. His skin, wherever it was exposed, was burned by the sun; even his lips were black, and his fair eyes looked quite startling in so dark a face. Of all the beggar-men I had ever seen or imagined, he was the most ragged. He was clothed in tatters of old ship's canvas and old sea-cloth, and this extraordinary patchwork was all held together by a system of the most varied and mismatched fastenings—brass buttons, bits of stick, and loops of tarry gasket. Around his waist he wore an old brass-buckled leather belt, which was the one solid thing in his whole outfit.
"Three years!" I cried. "Were you shipwrecked?"
"Nay, mate," he said; "marooned."

I had heard the word, and I knew it meant a horrible kind of punishment common enough among the buccaneers, in which the offender is put ashore with a little powder and shot and left behind on some desolate, distant island.

"Marooned three years ago," he went on, "and I've lived on goats since then, and berries, and oysters. Wherever a man is, says I, a man can do for himself. But, mate, my heart is sore for Christian food. You wouldn't happen to have a piece of cheese on you, now, would you? No? Well, many's the long night I've dreamed of cheese—toasted, mostly—and woke up again, and here I were."
"If ever I can get aboard again," I said, "you shall have cheese by the stone."

All this time he had been feeling the fabric of my jacket, smoothing my hands, looking at my boots, and generally, in the pauses of his talk, showing a childish pleasure at being in the presence of a fellow creature. But at my last words he perked up into a kind of startled slyness.
"If ever you can get aboard again, says you?" he repeated. "Why, now, who's to stop you?"
"Not you, I know," was my reply.
"And right you was," he cried. "Now you—what do you call yourself, mate?"
"Jim," I told him.

"Jim, Jim," he says, quite pleased apparently. "Well, now, Jim, I've lived that rough as you'd be ashamed to hear of. Now, for instance, you wouldn't think I'd had a pious mother—to look at me?" he asked.
"Why, no, not particularly," I answered.

"Ah, well," he said, "but I had—_re_markable pious. And I was a civil, pious boy, and could rattle off my catechism so fast you couldn't tell one word from another. And here's what it come to, Jim, and it begun with playing pitch-and-toss on the blessed gravestones! That's what it begun with, but it went further than that; and so my mother told me, and predicked the whole thing, she did, the pious woman! But it were Providence that put me here. I've thought it all out on this lonely island, and I'm back on piety. You won't catch me tasting rum much, but just a thimbleful for luck, of course, the first chance I have. I'm bound to be good, and I see the way to. And, Jim"—looking all around him and lowering his voice to a whisper—"I'm rich."

I felt sure by now that the poor fellow had gone crazy in his solitude, and I suppose I must have shown it in my face, for he repeated the statement hotly: "Rich! Rich! I says. And I'll tell you what: I'll make a man of you, Jim. Ah, Jim, you'll bless your stars, you will, you was the first that found me!"
And at this there suddenly came a lowering shadow over his face, and he tightened his grip on my hand and raised a forefinger threateningly before my eyes.
"Now, Jim, you tell me true: that ain't Flint's ship?" he asked.
At this I had a happy inspiration. I began to believe I had found an ally, and I answered him at once.
"It's not Flint's ship, and Flint is dead; but I'll tell you true, since you ask me—there are some of Flint's hands aboard; worse luck for the rest of us."
"Not a man—with one—leg?" he gasped.
"Silver?" I asked.
"Ah, Silver!" he says. "That were his name."
"He's the cook, and the ringleader too."
He was still holding me by the wrist, and at that he gave it quite a wring.
"If you was sent by Long John," he said, "I'm as good as pork, and I know it. But where was you, do you suppose?"

I made up my mind in a moment, and by way of answer told him the whole story of our voyage and the fix we were in. He listened with the keenest interest, and when I had finished he patted me on the head.

"You're a good lad, Jim," he said; "and you're all in a clove hitch, ain't you? Well, you just put your trust in Ben Gunn—Ben Gunn's the man to do it. Would you think it likely, now, that your squire would prove a generous-minded one in case of help—him being in a clove hitch, as you remark?"
I told him the squire was the most generous of men.

"Aye, but you see," returned Ben Gunn, "I didn't mean giving me a gate to keep, and a suit of livery clothes, and such; that's not my mark, Jim. What I mean is, would he be likely to come down to the tune of, say, one thousand pounds out of money that's as good as a man's own already?"
"I am sure he would," I said. "As it was, all hands were to share."
"AND a passage home?" he added with a look of great shrewdness.
"Why," I cried, "the squire's a gentleman. And besides, if we got rid of the others, we'd need you to help work the vessel home."
"Ah," he said, "so you would." And he seemed very much relieved.

"Now, I'll tell you what," he went on. "So much I'll tell you, and no more. I were in Flint's ship when he buried the treasure; he and six along—six strong seamen. They was ashore nigh on a week, and us standing off and on in the old Walrus. One fine day up went the signal, and here come Flint by himself in a little boat, and his head done up in a blue scarf. The sun was getting up, and mortal white he looked about the cutwater. But there he was, you mind, and the six all dead—dead and buried. How he done it, not a man aboard us could make out. It was battle, murder, and sudden death, leastways—him against six. Billy Bones was the mate; Long John, he was quartermaster; and they asked him where the treasure was. 'Ah,' says he, 'you can go ashore, if you like, and stay,' he says; 'but as for the ship, she'll beat up for more, by thunder!' That's what he said."

"Well, I was in another ship three years back, and we sighted this island. 'Boys,' said I, 'here's Flint's treasure; let's land and find it.' The cap'n was displeased at that, but my messmates were all of a mind and landed. Twelve days they looked for it, and every day they had a worse word for me, until one fine morning all hands went aboard. 'As for you, Benjamin Gunn,' says they, 'here's a musket,' they says, 'and a spade, and pick-axe. You can stay here and find Flint's money for yourself,' they says."

"Well, Jim, three years have I been here, and not a bite of Christian diet from that day to this. But now, you look here; look at me. Do I look like a man before the mast? No, says you. Nor I weren't, neither, I says."
And with that he winked and pinched me hard.

"Just you mention them words to your squire, Jim," he went on. "Nor he weren't, neither—that's the words. Three years he were the man of this island, light and dark, fair and rain; and sometimes he would maybe think upon a prayer (says you), and sometimes he would maybe think of his old mother, so be as she's alive (you'll say); but the most part of Gunn's time (this is what you'll say)—the most part of his time was took up with another matter. And then you'll give him a nip, like I do."
And he pinched me again in the most confidential manner.

"Then," he went on, "then you'll up, and you'll say this: Gunn is a good man (you'll say), and he puts a precious sight more confidence—a precious sight, mind that—in a gen'leman born than in these gen'lemen of fortune, having been one hisself."
"Well," I said, "I don't understand one word that you've been saying. But that's neither here nor there; for how am I to get on board?"

"Ah," he said, "that's the hitch, for sure. Well, there's my boat, that I made with my two hands. I keep her under the white rock. If the worst come to the worst, we might try that after dark. Hi!" he broke out. "What's that?"
For just then, although the sun still had an hour or two to run, all the echoes of the island woke and bellowed to the thunder of a cannon.
"They have begun to fight!" I cried. "Follow me."
And I began to run toward the anchorage, my terrors all forgotten, while close at my side the marooned man in his goatskins trotted easily and lightly.

"Left, left," he says; "keep to your left hand, mate Jim! Under the trees with you! Theer's where I killed my first goat. They don't come down here now; they're all mastheaded on them mountings for the fear of Benjamin Gunn. Ah! And there's the cetemery"—cemetery, he must have meant. "You see the mounds? I come here and prayed, nows and thens, when I thought maybe a Sunday would be about doo. It weren't quite a chapel, but it seemed more solemn like; and then, says you, Ben Gunn was short-handed—no chapling, nor so much as a Bible and a flag, you says."
So he kept talking as I ran, neither expecting nor receiving any answer.
The cannon-shot was followed after a considerable interval by a volley of small arms.
Another pause, and then, not a quarter of a mile in front of me, I saw the Union Jack flutter in the air above a wood.

chapters.title: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: How the Ship Was Abandoned
paragraphs: It was around half past one—three bells in sailor's language—when the two boats left the Hispaniola for shore. The captain, the squire, and I were talking things over in the cabin. If there had been any breath of wind, we would have fallen on the six mutineers still aboard, slipped our cable, and made for sea. But the wind was gone; and to make our helplessness complete, Hunter came down with the news that Jim Hawkins had slipped into a boat and gone ashore with the rest.

It never crossed our minds to doubt Jim Hawkins, but we were alarmed for his safety. With the men in the mood they were in, it seemed an even chance whether we'd ever see the lad again. We ran up on deck. The pitch was bubbling in the seams; the foul stench of the place turned my stomach; if ever a man smelled fever and dysentery, it was in that wretched anchorage. The six scoundrels sat grumbling under a sail in the forecastle; ashore, we could see the gigs tied up and a man sitting in each, close to where the river runs in. One of them was whistling "Lillibullero."
Waiting was a strain, and it was decided that Hunter and I should go ashore in the jolly-boat to gather information.

The gigs had pulled to their right, but Hunter and I rowed straight in, heading for the stockade marked on the chart. The two men left guarding their boats seemed thrown into a bustle by our appearance; "Lillibullero" stopped, and I could see the pair debating what they ought to do. If they had gone and told Silver, everything might have turned out differently; but they had their orders, I suppose, and decided to sit quietly where they were and pick up "Lillibullero" again.

There was a slight bend in the coast, and I steered so as to put it between us; even before we landed, we had lost sight of the gigs. I jumped out and came as near to running as I dared, with a big silk handkerchief under my hat to keep cool and a pair of pistols primed and ready for safety.
I hadn't gone a hundred yards when I reached the stockade.

This was how it stood: a spring of clear water rose almost at the top of a knoll. On the knoll itself, enclosing the spring, they had built a stout log-house big enough to hold forty people in a pinch, with loopholes for muskets on every side. All around it they had cleared a wide space, and the whole thing was finished off by a palisade six feet high, with no door or opening, too strong to pull down without time and tools, and too open to give attackers any cover. The people inside the log-house had every advantage; they stood quietly in shelter and shot the others like partridges. All they needed was a good watch and food; short of a complete surprise, they could have held the place against a regiment.

What particularly caught my eye was the spring. For although we had a decent enough position in the cabin of the Hispaniola, with plenty of arms and ammunition, things to eat, and excellent wines, one thing had been overlooked—we had no water. I was thinking this over when the cry of a man at the point of death came ringing across the island. I was no stranger to violent death—I have served his Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland, and took a wound myself at Fontenoy—but I can tell you my pulse jumped. "Jim Hawkins is gone," was my first thought.

It means something to have been an old soldier, but more still to have been a doctor. There's no time to dawdle in our work. So I made up my mind on the spot, and without losing a moment returned to the shore and jumped aboard the jolly-boat.
By good fortune Hunter was a strong oar. We made the water fly, and the boat was soon alongside and I was back aboard the schooner.

I found them all shaken, as was only natural. The squire was sitting down, white as a sheet, thinking of the harm he had led us into, the good soul! And one of the six forecastle hands was little better.
"There's a man," says Captain Smollett, nodding toward him, "new to this work. He came near to fainting, doctor, when he heard the cry. One more touch of the rudder and that man would join us."
I told my plan to the captain, and between us we worked out the details of carrying it out.

We posted old Redruth in the gallery between the cabin and the forecastle, with three or four loaded muskets and a mattress for protection. Hunter brought the boat round under the stern-port, and Joyce and I set to work loading her with tins of powder, muskets, bags of biscuits, kegs of pork, a cask of cognac, and my invaluable medicine chest.
Meanwhile, the squire and the captain stayed on deck, and the captain hailed the coxswain, who was the leading man aboard.
"Mr. Hands," he said, "here are two of us with a pair of pistols each. If any one of you six gives a signal of any kind, that man is dead."
