They were considerably taken aback, and after a brief consultation they all tumbled down the fore companion, thinking no doubt to take us from the rear. But when they saw Redruth waiting for them in the barred gallery, they turned about at once, and a head popped out again on deck.
"Down, dog!" cries the captain.
And the head ducked back again; for the time being, we heard no more of these six very faint-hearted seamen.

By this time, tossing things in as they came, we had loaded the jolly-boat as much as we dared. Joyce and I climbed out through the stern-port, and we made for shore again as fast as oars could take us.

This second trip fairly woke up the watchers along the shore. "Lillibullero" was dropped again; and just before we lost sight of them behind the little point, one of them whipped ashore and disappeared. I half thought of changing my plan and destroying their boats, but I was afraid that Silver and the others might be close at hand, and we might lose everything by trying for too much.

We soon touched land at the same spot as before and set to provisioning the block house. All three of us made the first journey, heavily loaded, and tossed our stores over the palisade. Then, leaving Joyce to guard them—one man, to be sure, but with half a dozen muskets—Hunter and I returned to the jolly-boat and loaded ourselves once more. So we went on without stopping to catch breath, until the whole cargo was inside; then the two servants took up their position in the block house, and I, with all my strength, sculled back to the Hispaniola.

That we should have risked a second boatload sounds more daring than it really was. They had the advantage of numbers, of course, but we had the advantage of arms. Not one of the men ashore had a musket, and before they could get within pistol range, we flattered ourselves we'd be able to give a good account of half a dozen at least.

The squire was waiting for me at the stern window, all his faintness gone. He caught the painter and made it fast, and we set to loading the boat for our very lives. Pork, powder, and biscuit made up the cargo, with only a musket and cutlass apiece for the squire and me and Redruth and the captain. The rest of the arms and powder we dropped overboard in two and a half fathoms of water, so that we could see the bright steel shining far below us in the sun, on the clean sandy bottom.

By now the tide was beginning to ebb, and the ship was swinging round on her anchor. Voices were faintly heard hallooing in the direction of the two gigs; and though that reassured us about Joyce and Hunter, who were well off to the east, it warned our party to be off.
Redruth retreated from his place in the gallery and dropped into the boat, which we then brought round to the ship's counter to be handier for Captain Smollett.
"Now, men," said he, "do you hear me?"
There was no answer from the forecastle.
"It's to you, Abraham Gray—it's to you I'm speaking."
Still no reply.

"Gray," Mr. Smollett went on, a little louder, "I am leaving this ship, and I order you to follow your captain. I know you're a good man at heart, and I dare say not one of the rest of you is as bad as he makes out. I have my watch here in my hand; I give you thirty seconds to join me."
There was a pause.
"Come, my fine fellow," the captain continued; "don't hang back so long. I'm risking my life and the lives of these good gentlemen with every second that passes."
There was a sudden scuffle, a sound of blows, and out burst Abraham Gray with a knife cut on the side of his cheek, and came running to the captain like a dog to the whistle.
"I'm with you, sir," he said.
And the next moment he and the captain had dropped aboard with us, and we had shoved off and were under way.
We were clear of the ship, but not yet ashore at our stockade.

chapters.title: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: The Jolly-boat’s Last Trip
paragraphs: This fifth trip was very different from any of the others. To begin with, the little nutshell of a boat we were in was seriously overloaded. Five grown men, three of them—Trelawney, Redruth, and the captain—over six feet tall, was already more than she was meant to carry. Add the powder, pork, and bread-bags to that. The gunwale was dipping at the stern. Several times we shipped a little water, and my breeches and the tails of my coat were soaking wet before we had gone a hundred yards.
The captain made us trim the boat, and we got her riding a little more evenly. Even so, we were afraid to breathe.

In the second place, the ebb was now running—a strong rippling current flowing westward through the basin, and then south and out to sea down the straits we had entered by that morning. Even the ripples were a danger to our overloaded craft, but the worst of it was that we were swept off our true course and away from our proper landing-place behind the point. If we let the current have its way, we'd come ashore beside the gigs, where the pirates might appear at any moment.

"I can't keep her head pointed for the stockade, sir," I said to the captain. I was steering, while he and Redruth, two fresh men, were at the oars. "The tide keeps washing her down. Could you pull a little harder?"
"Not without swamping the boat," he said. "You must bear up, sir, if you please—bear up until you see you're gaining."
I tried, and discovered by experiment that the tide kept sweeping us westward until I had laid her head due east, or just about at right angles to the way we needed to go.
"We'll never reach the shore at this rate," I said.

"If it's the only course we can hold, sir, we must hold it," the captain replied. "We must keep upstream. You see, sir," he went on, "if we once dropped to leeward of the landing-place, it's hard to say where we'd end up, besides the chance of being boarded by the gigs; the way we're going, the current must slacken, and then we can work back along the shore."
"The current's less already, sir," said the man Gray, who was sitting in the fore-sheets; "you can ease her off a bit."
"Thank you, my man," I said, just as if nothing had happened, for we had all quietly made up our minds to treat him as one of us.
Suddenly the captain spoke up again, and I thought his voice was a little changed.
"The gun!" he said.
"I've thought of that," I said, for I felt sure he was thinking of a bombardment of the fort. "They could never get the gun ashore, and if they did, they could never haul it through the woods."
"Look astern, doctor," the captain replied.

We had completely forgotten the long nine; and there, to our horror, were the five rogues busy around her, stripping off her jacket—as they called the stout tarpaulin cover she sailed under. Not only that, but it flashed into my mind at the same moment that the round-shot and the powder for the gun had been left behind, and one stroke of an axe would put it all into the possession of the villains aboard.
"Israel was Flint's gunner," said Gray hoarsely.

At any risk, we put the boat's head straight for the landing-place. By this time we had got so far out of the run of the current that we kept steerage way even at our necessarily gentle pace of rowing, and I could hold her steady for the goal. But the worst of it was that with the course I now held, we turned our broadside instead of our stern toward the Hispaniola and offered a target like a barn door.
I could hear as well as see that brandy-faced rascal Israel Hands dropping a round-shot onto the deck.
"Who's the best shot?" asked the captain.
"Mr. Trelawney, far and away," said I.
"Mr. Trelawney, would you please pick off one of these men for me, sir? Hands, if possible," said the captain.
Trelawney was as cool as steel. He checked the priming of his gun.
"Now," cried the captain, "easy with that gun, sir, or you'll swamp the boat. All hands stand by to trim her when he takes aim."
The squire raised his gun, the rowing stopped, and we leaned over to the other side to keep the balance, and the whole thing was managed so nicely that we didn't ship a drop.

By this time, they had the gun slewed round on its swivel, and Hands, who was at the muzzle with the rammer, was the most exposed as a result. However, we had no luck, for just as Trelawney fired, down he stooped, the ball whistled over him, and it was one of the other four who fell.

The cry he gave was echoed not only by his companions on board but by a great number of voices from the shore, and looking in that direction I saw the other pirates pouring out from among the trees and tumbling into their places in the boats.
"Here come the gigs, sir," I said.
"Give way, then," cried the captain. "We mustn't mind if we swamp her now. If we can't get ashore, it's all up."
"Only one of the gigs is being manned, sir," I added; "the crew of the other is most likely going round by the shore to cut us off."

"They'll have a hot run, sir," the captain returned. "Jack ashore, you know. It's not them I worry about; it's the round-shot. Carpet bowls! My lady's maid couldn't miss. Tell us, squire, when you see the match, and we'll hold water."

In the meantime we had been making headway at a good pace for a boat so overloaded, and we had shipped little water in the process. We were close in now; thirty or forty strokes and we'd beach her, for the ebb had already exposed a narrow belt of sand below the clustering trees. The gig was no longer to be feared; the little point had already hidden it from our view. The ebb-tide, which had so cruelly delayed us, was now making amends and delaying our pursuers. The one source of danger left was the gun.
"If I dared," said the captain, "I'd stop and pick off another man."
But it was plain they meant to let nothing delay their shot. They had never so much as glanced at their fallen comrade, though he wasn't dead, and I could see him trying to crawl away.
"Ready!" cried the squire.
"Hold!" cried the captain, quick as an echo.

And he and Redruth backed with a great heave that drove her stern bodily underwater. The report came in at the same instant. This was the first that Jim heard, since the sound of the squire's shot hadn't reached him. Where the ball passed, none of us could say precisely, but I suspect it must have been over our heads, and the wind of it may have contributed to our disaster.

At any rate, the boat sank by the stern, quite gently, in three feet of water, leaving the captain and me facing each other, still on our feet. The other three took complete headers, and came up again drenched and bubbling.

So far there was no great harm done. No lives were lost, and we could wade ashore in safety. But all our stores were at the bottom, and to make things worse, only two guns out of five were still fit for service. Mine I had snatched up from my knees and held over my head, by a kind of instinct. As for the captain, he had carried his over his shoulder by a bandoleer, and like a wise man, lock uppermost. The other three had gone down with the boat.

To add to our worries, we already heard voices drawing close to us in the woods along the shore, and we had not only the danger of being cut off from the stockade in our half-crippled state but also the fear that, if Hunter and Joyce were attacked by half a dozen men, they might not have the sense and steadiness to stand firm. Hunter was steady, that we knew; Joyce was a doubtful case—a pleasant, polite man for a valet and for brushing one's clothes, but not entirely cut out for a man of war.
With all this on our minds, we waded ashore as fast as we could, leaving behind us the poor jolly-boat and a good half of all our powder and provisions.

chapters.title: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: End of the First Day’s Fighting
paragraphs: We made our best speed across the strip of wood that now lay between us and the stockade, and at every step we took the voices of the buccaneers rang nearer. Soon we could hear their footfalls as they ran and the cracking of branches as they pushed through a patch of thicket.
I began to see we were in for a real fight, and checked the priming of my gun.
"Captain," I said, "Trelawney is the dead shot. Give him your gun; his own is useless."

They exchanged guns, and Trelawney, silent and cool as he had been from the start of the commotion, paused on his heel for a moment to make sure everything was fit for service. At the same time, noticing that Gray was unarmed, I handed him my cutlass. It did all our hearts good to see him spit on his hand, knit his brows, and make the blade sing through the air. It was plain from every line of his body that our new hand was worth his salt.

Forty paces farther on, we reached the edge of the wood and saw the stockade in front of us. We struck the enclosure about the middle of the south side, and almost at the same moment seven mutineers—Job Anderson, the boatswain, at their head—appeared in full cry at the southwestern corner.

They paused as if taken aback, and before they recovered, not only the squire and I, but Hunter and Joyce from the block house, had time to fire. The four shots came in a rather scattered volley, but they did the job: one of the enemy actually fell, and the rest, without hesitation, turned and plunged into the trees.
After reloading, we walked down the outside of the palisade to check on the fallen enemy. He was stone dead—shot through the heart.

We were beginning to rejoice over our success when, just at that moment, a pistol cracked in the bush, a ball whistled close past my ear, and poor Tom Redruth stumbled and fell his full length on the ground. The squire and I both returned the shot, but as we had nothing to aim at, we probably only wasted powder. Then we reloaded and turned our attention to poor Tom.
The captain and Gray were already examining him, and I saw at a glance that all was over.

I believe the readiness of our return volley had scattered the mutineers once more, for we were allowed without further trouble to hoist the poor old gamekeeper over the stockade and carry him, groaning and bleeding, into the log-house.

Poor old fellow, he hadn't uttered one word of surprise, complaint, fear, or even acceptance from the very start of our troubles until now, when we had laid him down in the log-house to die. He had lain like a Trojan behind his mattress in the gallery; he had followed every order silently, doggedly, and well; he was the oldest of our party by twenty years; and now, sullen, old, reliable servant, it was he that was to die.
The squire dropped down beside him on his knees and kissed his hand, crying like a child.
"Am I going, doctor?" he asked.
"Tom, my man," I said, "you're going home."
"I wish I'd had a lick at them with the gun first," he replied.
"Tom," said the squire, "say you forgive me, won't you?"
"Would that be respectful, from me to you, squire?" was the answer. "Howsoever, so be it, amen!"
After a little silence, he said he thought someone might read a prayer. "It's the custom, sir," he added apologetically. And not long after, without another word, he passed away.

Meanwhile the captain, whom I had noticed was wonderfully swollen about the chest and pockets, had turned out a great many varied stores—the British colours, a Bible, a coil of stoutish rope, pen, ink, the log-book, and several pounds of tobacco. He had found a longish fir-tree lying felled and trimmed in the enclosure, and with Hunter's help he had set it up at the corner of the log-house where the trunks crossed and made an angle. Then, climbing onto the roof, he had with his own hand bent and run up the colours.

This seemed to relieve him enormously. He went back into the log-house and set about counting up the stores as if nothing else existed. But he had an eye on Tom's passing all the same, and as soon as all was over, he came forward with another flag and reverently spread it over the body.

"Don't take it so hard, sir," he said, shaking the squire's hand. "All's well with him; no fear for a hand that's been shot down in his duty to captain and owner. It may not be good theology, but it's a fact."
Then he pulled me aside.
"Dr. Livesey," he said, "in how many weeks do you and the squire expect the consort?"

I told him it was a question not of weeks but of months, that if we weren't back by the end of August, Blandly was to send to find us, but neither sooner nor later. "You can work it out for yourself," I said.
"Why, yes," returned the captain, scratching his head; "and making a generous allowance, sir, for all the gifts of Providence, I'd say we're cutting it pretty close."
"How do you mean?" I asked.

"It's a pity, sir, that we lost that second load. That's what I mean," replied the captain. "As for powder and shot, we'll be all right. But the rations are short, very short—so short, Dr. Livesey, that we're perhaps as well without that extra mouth."
And he pointed to the dead body under the flag.
Just then, with a roar and a whistle, a round-shot passed high above the roof of the log-house and dropped far beyond us in the wood.
"Oho!" said the captain. "Blaze away! You've little enough powder already, my lads."
On the second try, the aim was better, and the ball came down inside the stockade, scattering a cloud of sand but doing no further damage.
"Captain," said the squire, "the house is quite invisible from the ship. It must be the flag they're aiming at. Wouldn't it be wiser to take it in?"

"Strike my colours!" cried the captain. "No, sir, not I"; and as soon as he had said the words, I think we all agreed with him. For it was not only a piece of stout, seamanly, good feeling; it was sound policy besides, and showed our enemies that we scorned their cannonade.

All through the evening they kept thundering away. Ball after ball flew over, or fell short, or kicked up the sand inside the enclosure, but they had to fire so high that the shot fell dead and buried itself in the soft sand. We had no ricochet to fear, and though one popped in through the roof of the log-house and out again through the floor, we soon got used to that kind of horse-play and minded it no more than a game of cricket.

"There is one good thing about all this," the captain observed; "the wood in front of us is probably clear. The ebb has been running a good while; our stores should be uncovered. Volunteers to go and bring in pork."

Gray and Hunter were the first to step forward. Well armed, they stole out of the stockade, but it turned out to be a useless mission. The mutineers were bolder than we had imagined, or else they put more trust in Israel's gunnery. For four or five of them were busy carrying off our stores and wading out with them to one of the gigs that lay close by, pulling an oar or so to hold her steady against the current. Silver was in the stern-sheets, in command; and every man of them was now armed with a musket from some secret magazine of their own.
The captain sat down to his log, and here is the beginning of the entry:

Alexander Smollett, master; David Livesey, ship's doctor; Abraham Gray, carpenter's mate; John Trelawney, owner; John Hunter and Richard Joyce, owner's servants, landsmen—being all that is left loyal of the ship's company—with stores for ten days at short rations, came ashore this day and flew British colours on the log-house in Treasure Island. Thomas Redruth, owner's servant, landsman, shot by the mutineers; James Hawkins, cabin-boy—
And at the same moment, I was wondering over poor Jim Hawkins' fate.
A hail from the land side.
"Somebody hailing us," said Hunter, who was on guard.
"Doctor! Squire! Captain! Hullo, Hunter, is that you?" came the shouts.
And I ran to the door just in time to see Jim Hawkins, safe and sound, come climbing over the stockade.

chapters.title: Narrative Resumed by Jim Hawkins: The Garrison in the Stockade
paragraphs: As soon as Ben Gunn saw the colours he came to a halt, stopped me by the arm, and sat down.
"Now," he said, "there's your friends, sure enough."
"Far more likely it's the mutineers," I answered.

"That!" he cried. "Why, in a place like this, where nobody puts in but gentlemen of fortune, Silver would fly the Jolly Roger, you can be sure of that. No, those are your friends. There's been blows, too, and I reckon your friends have had the best of it; and here they are ashore in the old stockade, that was made years and years ago by Flint. Ah, he was the man to have a head on his shoulders, was Flint! Barring rum, his match was never seen. He was afraid of none, not he; only Silver—Silver was that genteel."
"Well," said I, "that may be so, and if it is; all the more reason I should hurry on and join my friends."

"Nay, mate," returned Ben, "not you. You're a good boy, or I'm mistaken; but you're only a boy, all told. Now, Ben Gunn is fly. Rum wouldn't bring me there, where you're going—not rum wouldn't, till I see your born gentleman and gets it on his word of honour. And you won't forget my words; 'A precious sight (that's what you'll say), a precious sight more confidence'—and then nips him."
And he pinched me a third time with the same air of cleverness.

"And when Ben Gunn is wanted, you know where to find him, Jim. Just where you found him today. And whoever comes is to have a white thing in his hand, and he's to come alone. Oh! And you'll say this: 'Ben Gunn,' says you, 'has reasons of his own.'"
"Well," said I, "I think I understand. You have something to propose, and you want to see the squire or the doctor, and you're to be found where I found you. Is that all?"
"And when? says you," he added. "Why, from about noon observation to about six bells."
"Good," I said, "and now may I go?"

"You won't forget?" he asked anxiously. "Precious sight, and reasons of his own, says you. Reasons of his own; that's the mainstay; as between man and man. Well, then"—still holding me—"I reckon you can go, Jim. And, Jim, if you were to see Silver, you wouldn't go and sell Ben Gunn out? Wild horses wouldn't drag it from you? No, says you. And if those pirates camp ashore, Jim, what would you say but that there'd be widows in the morning?"

Here he was interrupted by a loud report, and a cannonball came tearing through the trees and pitched in the sand not a hundred yards from where we were talking. The next moment each of us had taken to his heels in a different direction.

For a good hour after, frequent reports shook the island, and balls kept crashing through the woods. I moved from one hiding-place to another, always pursued, or so it seemed to me, by these terrifying missiles. But toward the end of the bombardment, though I still didn't dare venture in the direction of the stockade, where the balls fell most often, I had begun, in a way, to pluck up my courage again, and after a long detour to the east, crept down among the shore-side trees.

The sun had just set, the sea breeze was rustling and tumbling in the woods and ruffling the grey surface of the anchorage; the tide was far out, too, and great tracts of sand lay uncovered; the air, after the heat of the day, chilled me through my jacket.

The Hispaniola still lay where she had anchored; but sure enough, there was the Jolly Roger—the black flag of piracy—flying from her peak. Even as I looked, there came another red flash and another report that sent the echoes clattering, and one more round-shot whistled through the air. It was the last of the cannonade.

I lay for some time watching the bustle that followed the attack. Men were smashing something with axes on the beach near the stockade—the poor jolly-boat, I learned later. Away near the mouth of the river, a great fire was glowing among the trees, and between that point and the ship one of the gigs kept coming and going, the men, whom I had seen so gloomy, shouting at the oars like children. But there was a sound in their voices that suggested rum.

At length I thought I might head back toward the stockade. I was pretty far down on the low, sandy spit that closes off the anchorage on the east, and joins Skeleton Island at half-tide; and now, as I rose to my feet, I saw, some distance further down the spit and rising from among low bushes, an isolated rock, fairly tall, and oddly white in colour. It struck me that this might be the white rock Ben Gunn had spoken of, and that some day or other a boat might be needed and I would know where to look.
Then I worked my way through the woods until I had regained the rear, or shoreward side, of the stockade, and was soon warmly welcomed by the loyal party.

I had soon told my story and began to look around me. The log-house was made of unsquared pine trunks—roof, walls, and floor. The floor stood in several places as much as a foot or a foot and a half above the surface of the sand. There was a porch at the door, and under this porch the little spring welled up into an artificial basin of a rather odd kind—none other than a great ship's iron kettle, with the bottom knocked out, and sunk "to her bearings," as the captain put it, in the sand.
Little had been left besides the framework of the house, but in one corner there was a stone slab laid down by way of a hearth and an old rusty iron basket to hold the fire.

The slopes of the knoll and all the inside of the stockade had been cleared of timber to build the house, and we could see by the stumps what a fine, tall grove had been destroyed. Most of the soil had been washed away or buried in drift after the trees were removed; only where the little stream ran down from the kettle did a thick bed of moss and a few ferns and small creeping bushes still grow green among the sand. Very close around the stockade—too close for defence, they said—the wood still grew high and dense, all fir on the land side, but toward the sea with a large mixture of live-oaks.

The cold evening breeze, which I mentioned, whistled through every chink in the rough building and sprinkled the floor with a constant rain of fine sand. There was sand in our eyes, sand in our teeth, sand in our suppers, sand dancing in the spring at the bottom of the kettle, for all the world like porridge starting to boil. Our chimney was a square hole in the roof; only a small part of the smoke found its way out, and the rest eddied around the house and kept us coughing and wiping our eyes.

Add to this that Gray, the new man, had his face tied up in a bandage for a cut he'd got breaking away from the mutineers, and that poor old Tom Redruth, still unburied, lay along the wall, stiff and stark, under the Union Jack.

If we had been allowed to sit idle, we would all have fallen into the blues, but Captain Smollett was never the man for that. All hands were called up before him, and he divided us into watches. The doctor, Gray, and I for one; the squire, Hunter, and Joyce on the other. Tired as we all were, two of us were sent out for firewood; two more were set to dig a grave for Redruth; the doctor was named cook; I was put on sentry at the door; and the captain himself went from one to another, keeping up our spirits and lending a hand wherever it was wanted.
From time to time the doctor came to the door for a little air and to rest his eyes, which were almost smoked out of his head, and whenever he did, he had a word for me.
"That man Smollett," he said once, "is a better man than I am. And when I say that, it means a lot, Jim."
Another time he came and was silent for a while. Then he put his head on one side and looked at me.
"Is this Ben Gunn a man?" he asked.
"I don't know, sir," I said. "I'm not very sure whether he's sane."

"If there's any doubt about the matter, he is," returned the doctor. "A man who has spent three years biting his nails on a desert island, Jim, can't expect to seem as sane as you or me. It isn't in human nature. Was it cheese, you said, that he had a fancy for?"
"Yes, sir, cheese," I answered.

"Well, Jim," says he, "just see the good that comes of being particular about your food. You've seen my snuff-box, haven't you? And you never saw me take snuff, the reason being that in my snuff-box I carry a piece of Parmesan cheese—a cheese made in Italy, very nutritious. Well, that's for Ben Gunn!"

Before supper was eaten we buried old Tom in the sand and stood around him for a while bare-headed in the breeze. A good deal of firewood had been brought in, but not enough for the captain's liking, and he shook his head over it and told us we "must get back to this tomorrow rather more lively." Then, when we had eaten our pork and each had a good stiff glass of brandy grog, the three chiefs got together in a corner to discuss our prospects.

It seems they were at their wits' end what to do, the stores being so low that we'd have been starved into surrender long before help could come. But our best hope, it was decided, was to kill off the buccaneers until they either hauled down their flag or ran off with the Hispaniola. From nineteen, they were already down to fifteen, two others were wounded, and one at least—the man shot beside the gun—severely wounded, if he wasn't dead. Every time we had a crack at them we were to take it, while saving our own lives with the utmost care. And besides that, we had two able allies—rum and the climate.

As for the first, though we were about half a mile away, we could hear them roaring and singing late into the night; and as for the second, the doctor staked his wig that, camped where they were in the marsh and with no remedies on hand, half of them would be flat on their backs within a week.
"So," he added, "if we're not all shot down first, they'll be glad enough to pack up in the schooner. She's still a ship, and they can get back to buccaneering, I suppose."
"First ship I ever lost," said Captain Smollett.
I was dead tired, as you can imagine; and when I finally got to sleep, which wasn't until after a great deal of tossing, I slept like a log.
The rest had long been up and had already breakfasted and added about half again as much to the pile of firewood when I was woken by a bustle and the sound of voices.
"Flag of truce!" I heard someone say; and then, immediately after, with a cry of surprise, "Silver himself!"
And at that I jumped up, and rubbing my eyes, ran to a loophole in the wall.

chapters.title: Silver’s Embassy
paragraphs: Sure enough, there were two men just outside the stockade, one of them waving a white cloth, the other—no less a person than Silver himself—standing calmly by.

It was still quite early, and the coldest morning I think I was ever out in—a chill that pierced to the marrow. The sky was bright and cloudless overhead, and the tops of the trees glowed rosily in the sun. But where Silver stood with his lieutenant, all was still in shadow, and they were wading knee-deep in a low white vapour that had crawled out of the marsh during the night. The chill and the vapour together told a poor tale of the island. It was plainly a damp, feverish, unhealthy spot.
"Keep indoors, men," said the captain. "Ten to one this is a trick."
Then he hailed the buccaneer.
"Who goes? Stand, or we fire."
"Flag of truce," cried Silver.

The captain was in the porch, keeping himself carefully out of the way of a treacherous shot, should any be meant. He turned and spoke to us: "Doctor's watch on the lookout. Dr. Livesey, take the north side, if you please; Jim, the east; Gray, west. The watch below, all hands to load muskets. Lively, men, and careful."
And then he turned back to the mutineers.
"And what do you want with your flag of truce?" he called.
This time it was the other man who replied.
"Cap'n Silver, sir, to come on board and make terms," he shouted.
"Cap'n Silver! Don't know him. Who's he?" cried the captain. And we could hear him adding to himself, "Cap'n, is it? My heart, here's promotion!"

Long John answered for himself. "Me, sir. These poor lads have chosen me cap'n, after your desertion, sir"—laying particular emphasis on the word "desertion." "We're willing to come to terms, if we can settle it, and no bones about it. All I ask is your word, Cap'n Smollett, to let me safe and sound out of this stockade, and one minute to get out of shot before a gun is fired."

"My man," said Captain Smollett, "I haven't the slightest desire to talk to you. If you wish to talk to me, you can come, that's all. If there's any treachery, it'll be on your side, and the Lord help you."
"That's enough, Cap'n," shouted Long John cheerily. "A word from you's enough. I know a gentleman, and you may lay to that."

We could see the man carrying the flag of truce trying to hold Silver back. Nor was that any wonder, seeing how cavalier the captain's answer had been. But Silver laughed at him aloud and slapped him on the back as if the idea of alarm were absurd. Then he advanced to the stockade, threw over his crutch, got a leg up, and with great vigour and skill managed to get over the fence and drop safely on the other side.

I'll admit I was far too caught up in what was going on to be of the slightest use as sentry; in fact, I'd already deserted my eastern loophole and crept up behind the captain, who had now sat down on the threshold, with his elbows on his knees, his head in his hands, and his eyes fixed on the water as it bubbled out of the old iron kettle in the sand. He was whistling "Come, Lasses and Lads."

Silver had a terribly hard time getting up the knoll. What with the steepness of the slope, the thick tree stumps, and the soft sand, he and his crutch were as helpless as a ship in stays. But he stuck to it like a man in silence, and at last arrived in front of the captain, whom he saluted in the handsomest style. He was decked out in his best; an immense blue coat, thick with brass buttons, hung as far as his knees, and a fine laced hat was set on the back of his head.
"Here you are, my man," said the captain, raising his head. "You'd better sit down."
"You ain't going to let me inside, Cap'n?" complained Long John. "It's a mighty cold morning, to be sure, sir, to sit outside on the sand."

"Why, Silver," said the captain, "if you had cared to be an honest man, you might have been sitting in your galley. It's your own doing. You're either my ship's cook—and then you were treated handsomely—or Cap'n Silver, a common mutineer and pirate, and then you can go hang!"

"Well, well, Cap'n," returned the sea-cook, sitting down as he was told on the sand, "you'll have to give me a hand up again, that's all. A sweet pretty place you have of it here. Ah, there's Jim! Top of the morning to you, Jim. Doctor, here's my service. Why, there you all are together like a happy family, in a manner of speaking."
"If you have anything to say, my man, better say it," said the captain.

"Right you were, Cap'n Smollett," replied Silver. "Duty is duty, to be sure. Well now, you look here, that was a good move of yours last night. I don't deny it was a good move. Some of you pretty handy with a handspike-end. And I'll not deny either that some of my people were shaken—maybe all were shaken; maybe I was shaken myself; maybe that's why I'm here for terms. But you mark me, Cap'n, it won't do twice, by thunder! We'll have to do sentry-go and ease off a point or so on the rum. Maybe you think we were all three sheets in the wind. But I'll tell you I was sober; I was only dog tired; and if I'd woken a second sooner, I'd have caught you in the act, I would. He wasn't dead when I got round to him, not he."
"Well?" says Captain Smollett, as cool as can be.

All that Silver said was a riddle to him, but you would never have guessed it from his tone. As for me, I began to have an inkling. Ben Gunn's last words came back to my mind. I began to suppose that he'd paid the buccaneers a visit while they all lay drunk together around their fire, and I reckoned up with glee that we now had only fourteen enemies to deal with.
"Well, here it is," said Silver. "We want that treasure, and we'll have it—that's our point! You'd just as soon save your lives, I reckon; and that's yours. You have a chart, haven't you?"
"That's as may be," replied the captain.

"Oh, well, you have, I know that," returned Long John. "You needn't be so gruff with a man; there ain't a particle of use in that, and you may lay to it. What I mean is, we want your chart. Now, I never meant you any harm, myself."
"That won't do with me, my man," interrupted the captain. "We know exactly what you meant to do, and we don't care, for now, you see, you can't do it."
And the captain looked at him calmly and went on filling a pipe.
"If Abe Gray—" Silver burst out.

"Avast there!" cried Mr. Smollett. "Gray told me nothing, and I asked him nothing; and what's more, I'd see you and him and this whole island blown clean out of the water into blazes first. So there's my mind for you, my man, on that."
This little flare of temper seemed to cool Silver down. He had been growing nettled before, but now he pulled himself together.

"Like enough," he said. "I'd set no limits on what gentlemen might consider shipshape, or might not, as the case might be. And seeing as how you're about to take a pipe, Cap'n, I'll make so bold as to do the same."

And he filled a pipe and lit it; and the two men sat silently smoking for quite a while, now looking each other in the face, now tamping their tobacco, now leaning forward to spit. It was as good as a play to watch them.

"Now," Silver resumed, "here it is. You give us the chart so we can get the treasure, and stop shooting poor seamen and staving in their heads while they're asleep. You do that, and we'll offer you a choice. Either you come aboard along with us, once the treasure's shipped, and then I'll give you my affidavy, upon my word of honour, to set you down somewhere safe ashore. Or, if that ain't to your fancy—some of my hands being rough and having old scores on account of hazing—then you can stay here, you can. We'll split stores with you, man for man; and I'll give my affidavy, as before, to speak the first ship I sight and send them here to pick you up. Now, you'll own that's talking. Handsomer you couldn't expect, not you. And I hope"—raising his voice—"that all hands in this block house will turn over my words, for what's spoken to one is spoken to all."
Captain Smollett rose from his seat and knocked out the ashes of his pipe into the palm of his left hand.
"Is that all?" he asked.
"Every last word, by thunder!" answered John. "Refuse that, and you've seen the last of me but musket-balls."

"Very good," said the captain. "Now you'll hear me. If you'll come up one by one, unarmed, I'll undertake to clap you all in irons and take you home to a fair trial in England. If you won't, my name is Alexander Smollett, I've flown my sovereign's colours, and I'll see you all to Davy Jones. You can't find the treasure. You can't sail the ship—there's not a man among you fit to sail the ship. You can't fight us—Gray there got away from five of you. Your ship's in irons, Master Silver; you're on a lee shore, and that's what you'll find. I stand here and tell you so; and they're the last good words you'll get from me, for in the name of heaven, I'll put a bullet in your back the next time I meet you. Tramp, my lad. Bundle out of this, please, hand over hand, and double quick."
Silver's face was a picture; his eyes started out of his head with rage. He shook the fire out of his pipe.
"Give me a hand up!" he cried.
"Not I," returned the captain.
"Who'll give me a hand up?" he roared.
Not a man among us moved. Growling the foulest curses, he crawled along the sand till he got hold of the porch and could hoist himself up again on his crutch. Then he spat into the spring.

"There!" he cried. "That's what I think of you. Before an hour's out, I'll stave in your old block house like a rum cask. Laugh, by thunder, laugh! Before an hour's out, you'll laugh on the other side. Them that die'll be the lucky ones."

And with a dreadful oath he stumbled off, ploughed down the sand, was helped across the stockade—after four or five failures—by the man with the flag of truce, and disappeared in an instant afterwards among the trees.

chapters.title: The Attack
paragraphs: As soon as Silver disappeared, the captain, who had been watching him closely, turned back to the inside of the house and found not one of us at his post but Gray. It was the first time we had ever seen him angry.

"Quarters!" he roared. And then, as we all slunk back to our places, "Gray," he said, "I'll put your name in the log; you've stood by your duty like a seaman. Mr. Trelawney, I'm surprised at you, sir. Doctor, I thought you had worn the king's coat! If that's how you served at Fontenoy, sir, you'd have been better in your berth."
The doctor's watch were all back at their loopholes, the rest were busy loading the spare muskets, and every man with a red face, you may be sure, and a flea in his ear, as the saying goes.
The captain looked on for a while in silence. Then he spoke.

"My lads," he said, "I've given Silver a broadside. I pitched it in red-hot on purpose; and before the hour's out, as he said, we'll be boarded. We're outnumbered, I needn't tell you that, but we fight from shelter; and a minute ago I would have said we fought with discipline. I've no doubt at all that we can drub them, if you choose."
Then he made the rounds and saw, as he said, that all was clear.

On the two short sides of the house, east and west, there were only two loopholes; on the south side, where the porch was, two again; and on the north side, five. There was a round score of muskets for the seven of us; the firewood had been built into four piles—tables, you might say—one about the middle of each side, and on each of these tables some ammunition and four loaded muskets were laid ready to the defenders' hand. In the middle, the cutlasses were laid out in a row.
"Toss out the fire," said the captain; "the chill is past, and we mustn't have smoke in our eyes."
The iron fire-basket was carried bodily out by Mr. Trelawney, and the embers were smothered in sand.

"Hawkins hasn't had his breakfast. Hawkins, help yourself, and back to your post to eat it," Captain Smollett went on. "Lively, now, my lad; you'll need it before you're done. Hunter, serve out a round of brandy to all hands."
And while this was going on, the captain finished, in his own mind, the plan of defence.

"Doctor, you will take the door," he resumed. "Mind, don't expose yourself; keep within, and fire through the porch. Hunter, take the east side, there. Joyce, you stand by the west, my man. Mr. Trelawney, you are the best shot—you and Gray will take this long north side, with the five loopholes; that's where the danger is. If they can get up to it and fire in on us through our own ports, things would start to look dirty. Hawkins, neither you nor I are much use at the shooting; we'll stand by to load and lend a hand."

As the captain had said, the chill was past. As soon as the sun had climbed above our ring of trees, it fell with all its force on the clearing and drank up the vapours in a draught. Soon the sand was baking and the resin melting in the logs of the block house. Jackets and coats were flung aside, shirts thrown open at the neck and rolled up to the shoulders; and we stood there, each at his post, in a fever of heat and anxiety.
An hour passed.
"Hang them!" said the captain. "This is as dull as the doldrums. Gray, whistle for a wind."
And just at that moment came the first news of the attack.
"If you please, sir," said Joyce, "if I see anyone, am I to fire?"
"I told you so!" cried the captain.
"Thank you, sir," returned Joyce with the same quiet civility.

Nothing followed for a time, but the remark had put us all on the alert, straining ears and eyes—the musketeers with their pieces balanced in their hands, the captain out in the middle of the block house with his mouth set tight and a frown on his face.

So some seconds passed, until suddenly Joyce whipped up his musket and fired. The report had barely died away before it was repeated and repeated from outside in a scattered volley, shot after shot, like a string of geese, from every side of the enclosure. Several bullets struck the log-house, but not one came inside; and as the smoke cleared and vanished, the stockade and the woods around it looked as quiet and empty as before. Not a bough waved, not the gleam of a musket-barrel betrayed the presence of our foes.
"Did you hit your man?" asked the captain.
"No, sir," replied Joyce. "I don't think so, sir."
"Next best thing is to tell the truth," muttered Captain Smollett. "Load his gun, Hawkins. How many would you say there were on your side, doctor?"
"I know exactly," said Dr. Livesey. "Three shots were fired on this side. I saw the three flashes—two close together—one farther to the west."
"Three!" the captain repeated. "And how many on yours, Mr. Trelawney?"

But this was not so easily answered. Many had come from the north—seven by the squire's count, eight or nine by Gray's. From the east and west only a single shot had been fired. It was plain, therefore, that the attack would come from the north, and that on the other three sides we were only to be harassed by a show of hostilities. But Captain Smollett made no change in his arrangements. If the mutineers succeeded in crossing the stockade, he argued, they'd take possession of any unguarded loophole and shoot us down like rats in our own stronghold.

We had little time left for thought. Suddenly, with a loud huzza, a small cloud of pirates leapt from the woods on the north side and ran straight at the stockade. At the same moment, fire was opened again from the woods, and a rifle ball sang through the doorway and knocked the doctor's musket to bits.

The boarders swarmed over the fence like monkeys. Squire and Gray fired again and yet again; three men fell, one forward into the enclosure, two back on the outside. But of these, one was evidently more frightened than hurt, for he was on his feet again in a flash and instantly disappeared among the trees.

Two had bitten the dust, one had fled, four had got their footing inside our defences, while from the shelter of the woods seven or eight men, each evidently supplied with several muskets, kept up a hot though useless fire on the log-house.

The four who had boarded made straight for the building, shouting as they ran, and the men among the trees shouted back to encourage them. Several shots were fired, but the marksmen were in such a hurry that not one seems to have taken effect. In a moment, the four pirates had swarmed up the mound and were upon us.
The head of Job Anderson, the boatswain, appeared at the middle loophole.
"At them, all hands—all hands!" he roared in a voice of thunder.

At the same moment, another pirate grabbed Hunter's musket by the muzzle, wrenched it from his hands, yanked it out through the loophole, and with one stunning blow laid the poor fellow senseless on the floor. Meanwhile a third, running unharmed all around the house, suddenly appeared in the doorway and fell with his cutlass on the doctor.
Our position was utterly reversed. A moment ago we were firing, under cover, at an exposed enemy; now it was we who were exposed and could not return a blow.
The log-house was full of smoke, to which we owed our relative safety. Cries and confusion, the flashes and reports of pistol-shots, and one loud groan rang in my ears.
"Out, lads, out, and fight them in the open! Cutlasses!" cried the captain.

I snatched a cutlass from the pile, and someone else, snatching another at the same time, gave me a cut across the knuckles that I hardly felt. I dashed out of the door into the clear sunlight. Someone was close behind, I knew not whom. Right in front, the doctor was chasing his attacker down the hill, and just as my eyes fell on him, he beat down his guard and sent him sprawling on his back with a great slash across the face.
"Round the house, lads! Round the house!" cried the captain; and even in the hurly-burly, I noticed a change in his voice.

Mechanically, I obeyed, turned east, and with my cutlass raised, ran round the corner of the house. Next moment I was face to face with Anderson. He roared aloud, and his hanger went up above his head, flashing in the sunlight. I hadn't time to be afraid, but as the blow still hung overhead, I leapt in an instant to one side, and missing my footing in the soft sand, rolled headlong down the slope.

When I had first sallied from the door, the other mutineers had already been swarming up the palisade to make an end of us. One man, in a red night-cap, with his cutlass in his mouth, had even got onto the top and thrown a leg across. Well, so short had been the interval that when I found my feet again everything was in the same posture, the fellow with the red night-cap still halfway over, another still just showing his head above the top of the stockade. And yet, in this breath of time, the fight was over and the victory was ours.

Gray, following close behind me, had cut down the big boatswain before he had time to recover from his last blow. Another had been shot at a loophole in the very act of firing into the house and now lay in agony, the pistol still smoking in his hand. A third, as I had seen, the doctor had disposed of with a single blow. Of the four who had scaled the palisade, only one remained unaccounted for, and he, having left his cutlass on the field, was now clambering out again with the fear of death upon him.
"Fire—fire from the house!" cried the doctor. "And you, lads, back into cover."

But his words went unheeded, no shot was fired, and the last boarder made good his escape and disappeared with the rest into the wood. In three seconds nothing remained of the attacking party but the five who had fallen, four on the inside and one on the outside of the palisade.
The doctor and Gray and I ran full speed for shelter. The survivors would soon be back where they had left their muskets, and at any moment the fire might start up again.

The house was by this time somewhat cleared of smoke, and we saw at a glance the price we had paid for victory. Hunter lay beside his loophole, stunned; Joyce by his, shot through the head, never to move again; while right in the centre, the squire was supporting the captain, one as pale as the other.
"The captain's wounded," said Mr. Trelawney.
"Have they run?" asked Mr. Smollett.
"All that could, you may be sure," returned the doctor; "but there are five of them who'll never run again."

"Five!" cried the captain. "Come, that's better. Five against three leaves us four to nine. That's better odds than we had at the start. We were seven to nineteen then, or thought we were, and that's as bad to bear." *

*The mutineers were soon down to only eight, for the man shot by Mr. Trelawney aboard the schooner died that same evening of his wound. But this was, of course, not known until later by the faithful party.

chapters.title: How I Began My Sea Adventure
paragraphs: The mutineers did not return—not so much as another shot came out of the woods. They had “got their rations for that day,” as the captain put it, and we had the place to ourselves and a quiet stretch to tend the wounded and prepare dinner. The squire and I cooked outside in spite of the danger, and even outside we could hardly tell what we were doing, because of the horror of the loud groans that reached us from the doctor’s patients.

Out of the eight men who had fallen in the action, only three still breathed—the pirate who had been shot at the loophole, Hunter, and Captain Smollett; and of these, the first two were as good as dead. The mutineer indeed died under the doctor’s knife, and Hunter, for all we could do, never recovered consciousness in this world. He lingered all day, breathing loudly like the old buccaneer at home in his apoplectic fit, but the bones of his chest had been crushed by the blow and his skull fractured in the fall, and some time in the following night, without sign or sound, he went to his Maker.

As for the captain, his wounds were serious indeed, but not life-threatening. No organ had been fatally injured. Anderson’s ball—for it was Job who shot him first—had broken his shoulder-blade and grazed the lung, though not badly; the second had only torn and displaced some muscles in his calf. He was sure to recover, the doctor said, but in the meantime, and for weeks to come, he must not walk nor move his arm, nor even speak when he could help it.
My own accidental cut across the knuckles was a flea-bite. Doctor Livesey patched it up with plaster and pulled my ears for me into the bargain.

After dinner the squire and the doctor sat by the captain’s side for a while in consultation; and when they had talked to their hearts’ content, it being then a little past noon, the doctor took up his hat and pistols, buckled on a cutlass, put the chart in his pocket, and with a musket over his shoulder crossed the palisade on the north side and set off briskly through the trees.

Gray and I were sitting together at the far end of the block house, to be out of earshot of our officers consulting; and Gray took his pipe out of his mouth and altogether forgot to put it back, so thunder-struck he was at this development.
“Why, in the name of Davy Jones,” said he, “is Dr. Livesey mad?”
“Why no,” says I. “He’s about the last man in this crew you’d say that of, I take it.”
“Well, shipmate,” said Gray, “mad he may not be; but if HE isn’t, you mark my words, I am.”
“I take it,” I replied, “the doctor has his idea; and if I am right, he’s going now to see Ben Gunn.”

I was right, as appeared later; but in the meantime, the house being stifling hot and the little patch of sand inside the palisade ablaze with midday sun, I began to get another thought into my head, which was not by any means so right. What I began to do was to envy the doctor walking in the cool shadow of the woods with the birds about him and the pleasant smell of the pines, while I sat grilling, with my clothes stuck to the hot resin, and so much blood about me and so many poor dead bodies lying all around that I felt a disgust of the place that was almost as strong as fear.

All the time I was washing out the block house, and then washing up the things from dinner, this disgust and envy kept growing stronger and stronger, till at last, being near a bread-bag, and no one then observing me, I took the first step towards my escapade and filled both pockets of my coat with biscuit.

I was a fool, if you like, and certainly I was about to do a foolish, over-bold thing; but I was determined to do it with all the precautions in my power. These biscuits, should anything befall me, would keep me, at least, from starving till far on in the next day.
The next thing I laid hold of was a brace of pistols, and as I already had a powder-horn and bullets, I felt myself well supplied with arms.

As for the scheme in my head, it was not a bad one in itself. I was to go down the sandy spit that divides the anchorage on the east from the open sea, find the white rock I had noticed last evening, and check whether it was there or not that Ben Gunn had hidden his boat—a thing quite worth doing, as I still believe. But as I was certain I should not be allowed to leave the enclosure, my only plan was to take French leave and slip out when nobody was watching, and that was so bad a way of doing it that it made the thing itself wrong. But I was only a boy, and I had made up my mind.

Well, as things at last fell out, I found an admirable opportunity. The squire and Gray were busy helping the captain with his bandages, the coast was clear, and I made a bolt for it over the stockade and into the thickest of the trees, and before my absence was noticed I was out of cry of my companions.
This was my second folly, far worse than the first, since I left only two sound men to guard the house; but like the first, it ended up helping to save all of us.

I took my way straight for the east coast of the island, since I was determined to go down the seaward side of the spit to avoid all chance of being seen from the anchorage. It was already late in the afternoon, although still warm and sunny. As I went on threading the tall woods, I could hear from far ahead of me not only the continuous thunder of the surf, but a certain tossing of foliage and grinding of boughs that told me the sea breeze had set in higher than usual. Soon cool draughts of air began to reach me, and a few steps further on I came out into the open edges of the grove, and saw the sea lying blue and sunny to the horizon and the surf tumbling and tossing its foam along the beach.

I have never seen the sea quiet round Treasure Island. The sun might blaze overhead, the air be without a breath, the surface smooth and blue, and still these great rollers would be running along all the outer coast, thundering and thundering by day and night; and I scarcely believe there is a single spot on the island where a man would be out of earshot of their noise.
I walked along beside the surf with great enjoyment till, thinking I had now got far enough south, I took the cover of some thick bushes and crept warily up to the ridge of the spit.

Behind me was the sea, in front the anchorage. The sea breeze, as though it had the sooner blown itself out by its unusual violence, was already at an end; it had been replaced by light, variable airs from the south and south-east, carrying great banks of fog; and the anchorage, under lee of Skeleton Island, lay still and leaden as when we first entered it. The HISPANIOLA, in that unbroken mirror, was exactly portrayed from the truck to the waterline, the Jolly Roger hanging from her peak.

Alongside her lay one of the gigs, Silver in the stern-sheets—him I could always recognize—while a couple of men were leaning over the stern bulwarks, one of them with a red cap—the very rogue I had seen some hours before stride-legged on the palisade. They were apparently talking and laughing, though at that distance—upwards of a mile—I could of course hear not a word of what was said. All at once there began the most horrid, unearthly screaming, which at first startled me badly, though I had soon recognized the voice of Captain Flint and even thought I could make out the bird by her bright plumage as she sat perched upon her master’s wrist.
Soon afterwards the jolly-boat shoved off and pulled for shore, and the man with the red cap and his comrade went below by the cabin companion.

Just about the same time, the sun had gone down behind the Spy-glass, and as the fog was collecting rapidly, it began to grow dark in earnest. I saw I must lose no time if I were to find the boat that evening.

The white rock, visible enough above the brush, was still some eighth of a mile further down the spit, and it took me a goodish while to come up with it, crawling, often on all fours, among the scrub. Night had almost come when I laid my hand on its rough sides. Right below it there was an exceedingly small hollow of green turf, hidden by banks and a thick underwood about knee-deep that grew there very plentifully; and in the centre of the dell, sure enough, a little tent of goat-skins, like what the gipsies carry about with them in England.

I dropped into the hollow, lifted the side of the tent, and there was Ben Gunn’s boat—home-made if ever anything was home-made; a crude, lop-sided framework of tough wood, and stretched over it a covering of goat-skin, with the hair on the inside. The thing was extremely small, even for me, and I can hardly imagine that it could have floated with a full-sized man on board. There was one thwart set as low as possible, a kind of stretcher in the bows, and a double paddle for propulsion.

I had not then seen a coracle, such as the ancient Britons made, but I have seen one since, and I can give you no fairer idea of Ben Gunn’s boat than by saying it was like the first and the worst coracle ever made by man. But the great advantage of the coracle it certainly did possess, for it was exceedingly light and portable.

Well, now that I had found the boat, you would have thought I had had enough of truantry for once, but in the meantime I had taken another notion and become so obstinately fond of it that I would have carried it out, I believe, in the teeth of Captain Smollett himself. This was to slip out under cover of night, cut the HISPANIOLA adrift, and let her drift ashore wherever she fancied. I had quite made up my mind that the mutineers, after their repulse that morning, had nothing nearer their hearts than to weigh anchor and put to sea; this, I thought, it would be a fine thing to prevent, and now that I had seen how they left their watchmen without a boat, I thought it might be done with little risk.

Down I sat to wait for darkness, and made a hearty meal of biscuit. It was a night out of ten thousand for my purpose. The fog had now buried all the heavens. As the last rays of daylight dwindled and disappeared, absolute blackness settled down on Treasure Island. And when at last I shouldered the coracle and groped my way stumblingly out of the hollow where I had supped, there were but two points of light visible on the whole anchorage.

One was the great fire on shore, by which the defeated pirates lay carousing in the swamp. The other, a mere blur of light upon the darkness, marked the position of the anchored ship. She had swung round to the ebb—her bow was now towards me—the only lights aboard were in the cabin, and what I saw was merely a reflection on the fog of the strong rays that streamed from the stern window.

The ebb had already been running for some time, and I had to wade through a long belt of swampy sand, where I sank several times above the ankle, before I came to the edge of the retreating water, and wading a little way in, with some strength and dexterity, set my coracle, keel downwards, on the surface.

chapters.title: The Ebb-tide Runs
paragraphs: The coracle — as I had every reason to learn before I was done with her — was a very safe boat for a person of my height and weight, both buoyant and clever in a seaway; but she was the most cross-grained, lopsided little craft to manage. Do what you would, she always drifted more sideways than anything else, and turning round and round was the maneuver she was best at. Even Ben Gunn himself has admitted she was “queer to handle till you knew her way.”

I certainly did not know her way. She turned in every direction except the one I needed to go; most of the time we were broadside on, and I am quite sure I would never have reached the ship at all if it had not been for the tide. By good luck, paddle as I might, the tide was still sweeping me down; and there lay the HISPANIOLA right in the fairway, hardly possible to miss.

First she loomed before me like a blot of something even blacker than the darkness, then her spars and hull began to take shape, and the next moment, it seemed (for the farther I went, the brisker the ebb current became), I was alongside her hawser and had taken hold of it.

The hawser was as taut as a bowstring, and the current so strong it pulled hard against her anchor. All around the hull, in the blackness, the rippling current bubbled and chattered like a little mountain stream. One cut with my seaman's knife and the HISPANIOLA would go humming away down the tide.

So far so good, but it then occurred to me that a taut hawser, suddenly cut, is a thing as dangerous as a kicking horse. Ten to one, if I were so foolhardy as to cut the HISPANIOLA loose from her anchor, the coracle and I would be knocked clean out of the water.

This brought me to a full stop, and if luck had not particularly favored me once again, I would have had to abandon my plan. But the light airs that had begun blowing from the southeast and south had shifted around after nightfall to the southwest. Just while I was thinking it over, a puff came, caught the HISPANIOLA, and forced her up into the current; and to my great joy, I felt the hawser slacken in my grasp, and the hand by which I held it dipped for a second under water.

With that I made up my mind, pulled out my knife, opened it with my teeth, and cut one strand after another, until the vessel hung by only two. Then I lay still, waiting to sever those last fibers when the tension was eased again by another breath of wind.

All this time I had heard the sound of loud voices from the cabin, but to tell the truth, my mind had been so taken up with other things that I had barely been listening. Now, however, with nothing else to do, I began to pay closer attention.

One I recognized as the coxswain's voice, Israel Hands, who had been Flint's gunner in former days. The other was, of course, my friend of the red nightcap. Both men were plainly the worse for drink, and they were still drinking, for even while I was listening, one of them, with a drunken shout, opened the stern window and threw something out, which I guessed to be an empty bottle. But they were not only tipsy; it was plain that they were furiously angry. Oaths flew like hailstones, and every now and then there came such an outburst that I thought it must surely end in blows. But each time the quarrel passed off and the voices grumbled lower for a while, until the next flare-up came and in its turn died away without result.

On shore I could see the glow of the great campfire burning warmly through the trees by the shoreline. Someone was singing, a dull, old, droning sailor's song, with a droop and a quaver at the end of every verse, and seemingly no end to it at all but the patience of the singer. I had heard it on the voyage more than once and remembered these words:
“But one man of her crew alive, What put to sea with seventy-five.”

And I thought it was a ditty rather too dolefully fitting for a company that had suffered such cruel losses that morning. But indeed, from what I saw, all these buccaneers were as callous as the sea they sailed on.
At last the breeze came; the schooner sidled and drew nearer in the dark; I felt the hawser slacken once more, and with a good, tough effort, I cut the last fibers through.

The breeze had little effect on the coracle, and I was almost instantly swept against the bows of the HISPANIOLA. At the same time, the schooner began to turn on her heel, spinning slowly, end for end, across the current.

I worked like a fiend, for I expected every moment to be swamped; and since I found I could not push the coracle straight off, I now shoved her directly astern. At last I was clear of my dangerous neighbor, and just as I gave the last push, my hands came across a light cord that was trailing overboard across the stern bulwarks. Instantly I grasped it.

Why I should have done so I can hardly say. At first it was mere instinct, but once I had it in my hands and found it fast, curiosity began to take over, and I decided I would have one look through the cabin window.

I pulled in hand over hand on the cord, and when I judged myself near enough, I rose at terrible risk to about half my height and thus commanded a view of the roof and a slice of the cabin's interior.

By now the schooner and her little consort were gliding fairly swiftly through the water; indeed, we had already drawn level with the campfire. The ship was talking, as sailors say, loudly, treading the countless ripples with a constant weltering splash; and until I got my eye above the window-sill I could not understand why the watchmen had given no alarm. One glance, however, was enough; and one glance was all I dared take from that unsteady skiff. It showed me Hands and his companion locked together in deadly wrestle, each with a hand upon the other's throat.

I dropped down onto the thwart again, none too soon, for I was nearly overboard. For the moment I could see nothing but those two furious, blood-flushed faces swaying together under the smoky lamp, and I shut my eyes to let them grow used to the darkness once more.
The endless ballad had come to an end at last, and the whole diminished company around the campfire had broken into the chorus I had heard so often:
“Fifteen men on the dead man's chest — Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum! Drink and the devil had done for the rest — Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

I was just thinking how busy drink and the devil were at that very moment in the cabin of the HISPANIOLA, when I was startled by a sudden lurch of the coracle. At the same instant, she yawed sharply and seemed to change her course. The speed, meanwhile, had strangely increased.

I opened my eyes at once. All around me were little ripples, combing over with a sharp, bristling sound and faintly phosphorescent. The HISPANIOLA herself, a few yards ahead in whose wake I was still being whirled along, seemed to stagger in her course, and I saw her spars toss a little against the blackness of the night; in fact, as I looked longer, I felt sure she was also wheeling to the southward.

I glanced over my shoulder, and my heart jumped against my ribs. There, right behind me, was the glow of the campfire. The current had turned at right angles, sweeping along with it the tall schooner and the little dancing coracle; ever quickening, ever bubbling higher, ever muttering louder, it went spinning through the narrows toward the open sea.

Suddenly the schooner ahead of me gave a violent yaw, turning, perhaps, twenty degrees; and almost at the same moment one shout followed another from on board; I could hear feet pounding on the companion ladder and I knew that the two drunkards had finally been interrupted in their quarrel and awakened to the disaster they were in.

I lay down flat in the bottom of that wretched skiff and devoutly commended my spirit to its Maker. At the end of the straits, I was sure we must fall into some bar of raging breakers, where all my troubles would be ended quickly; and though I might perhaps be able to bear dying, I could not bear to watch my fate as it came on.

So I must have lain for hours, continually battered back and forth on the swells, now and then wetted by flying spray, and never ceasing to expect death at the next plunge. Gradually weariness took hold of me; a numbness, an occasional stupor, fell upon my mind even in the middle of my terrors, until at last sleep came over me, and in my sea-tossed coracle I lay and dreamed of home and the old Admiral Benbow.

chapters.title: The Cruise of the Coracle
paragraphs: It was broad daylight when I awoke and found myself tossing at the southwest end of Treasure Island. The sun was up, but was still hidden from me behind the great bulk of the Spy-glass, which on this side dropped almost down to the sea in formidable cliffs.

Haulbowline Head and Mizzenmast Hill were at my elbow, the hill bare and dark, the head bound with cliffs forty or fifty feet high and fringed with great masses of fallen rock. I was barely a quarter of a mile to seaward, and my first thought was to paddle in and land.

That notion was soon given up. Among the fallen rocks the breakers spouted and bellowed; loud reverberations, heavy sprays flying and falling, followed one another from second to second; and I saw myself, if I ventured closer, dashed to death upon the rough shore or wasting my strength in vain trying to scale the overhanging crags.

Nor was that all, for crawling together on flat tables of rock or letting themselves drop into the sea with loud reports, I saw huge slimy monsters — soft snails, as it were, of incredible size — two or three score of them together, making the rocks echo with their barkings.

I have since understood that they were sea lions, and entirely harmless. But the look of them, added to the difficulty of the shore and the high running of the surf, was more than enough to disgust me with that landing place. I felt more willing to starve at sea than to face such dangers.

In the meantime I had a better chance, as I supposed, before me. North of Haulbowline Head, the land runs in a long way, leaving at low tide a long stretch of yellow sand. To the north of that, again, there comes another cape — Cape of the Woods, as it was marked on the chart — buried in tall green pines, which came down to the very edge of the sea.

I remembered what Silver had said about the current that sets northward along the whole west coast of Treasure Island, and seeing from my position that I was already under its influence, I preferred to leave Haulbowline Head behind me and save my strength for an attempt to land on the kinder-looking Cape of the Woods.
There was a great, smooth swell upon the sea. The wind blowing steady and gentle from the south, there was no clash between it and the current, and the billows rose and fell unbroken.

Had it been otherwise, I must long ago have perished; but as it was, it is surprising how easily and securely my little, light boat could ride. Often, as I still lay at the bottom and kept no more than an eye above the gunwale, I would see a big blue summit heaving close above me; yet the coracle would only bounce a little, dance as if on springs, and settle on the other side into the trough as lightly as a bird.

After a little while I began to grow very bold and sat up to try my skill at paddling. But even a small change in the placement of weight will produce violent changes in the behavior of a coracle. And I had hardly moved before the boat, abandoning at once her gentle dancing motion, ran straight down a slope of water so steep that it made me dizzy, and struck her nose, with a spout of spray, deep into the side of the next wave.

I was drenched and terrified, and fell instantly back into my old position, whereupon the coracle seemed to find her head again and led me as softly as before through the billows. It was plain she was not to be interfered with, and at that rate, since I could in no way influence her course, what hope did I have left of reaching land?

I began to be horribly frightened, but I kept my head, for all that. First, moving with all care, I gradually bailed out the coracle with my sea-cap; then, getting my eye once more above the gunwale, I set myself to studying how she managed to slip so quietly through the rollers.

I found that each wave, instead of the big, smooth glossy mountain it looks from shore or from a ship's deck, was for all the world like any range of hills on dry land, full of peaks and smooth places and valleys. The coracle, left to herself, turning from side to side, threaded, so to speak, her way through these lower parts and avoided the steep slopes and higher, toppling summits of the wave.

“Well, now,” I thought to myself, “it is plain I must lie where I am and not disturb the balance; but it is plain also that I can put the paddle over the side and from time to time, in smooth places, give her a shove or two toward land.” No sooner thought of than done. There I lay on my elbows in the most trying position, and every now and then gave a weak stroke or two to turn her head toward the shore.

It was very tiring and slow work, yet I did clearly gain ground; and as we drew near the Cape of the Woods, though I saw I must certainly miss that point, I had still made some hundred yards of easting. I was, indeed, close in. I could see the cool green treetops swaying together in the breeze, and I felt sure I would make the next promontory without fail.

It was about time, for I now began to be tormented by thirst. The glow of the sun from above, its thousandfold reflection from the waves, the sea water that fell and dried on me, caking my very lips with salt, combined to make my throat burn and my brain ache. The sight of the trees so near at hand had almost made me sick with longing, but the current had soon carried me past the point, and as the next stretch of sea opened out, I saw a sight that changed the nature of my thoughts.

Right in front of me, not half a mile away, I saw the HISPANIOLA under sail. I was sure, of course, that I would be taken; but I was so distressed for want of water that I scarcely knew whether to be glad or sorry at the thought, and long before I had reached a conclusion, surprise had taken complete possession of my mind and I could do nothing but stare and wonder.

The HISPANIOLA was under her mainsail and two jibs, and the beautiful white canvas shone in the sun like snow or silver. When I first sighted her, all her sails were drawing; she was holding a course about northwest, and I assumed the men on board were going round the island on their way back to the anchorage. Soon she began to fetch more and more to the westward, so that I thought they had spotted me and were going about in chase. At last, however, she fell right into the wind's eye, was taken dead aback, and stood there a while helpless, with her sails shivering.
“Clumsy fellows,” said I; “they must still be drunk as owls.” And I thought how Captain Smollett would have set them skipping.

Meanwhile the schooner gradually fell off and filled again on another tack, sailed swiftly for a minute or so, and brought up once more dead in the wind's eye. Again and again was this repeated. To and fro, up and down, north, south, east, and west, the HISPANIOLA sailed by swoops and dashes, and at each repetition ended as she had begun, with idly flapping canvas. It became plain to me that nobody was steering. And if so, where were the men? Either they were dead drunk or had deserted her, I thought, and perhaps if I could get on board I might return the vessel to her captain.

The current was carrying coracle and schooner southward at an equal rate. As for the schooner's sailing, it was so wild and intermittent, and she hung each time so long in irons, that she certainly gained nothing, if she did not even lose. If only I dared sit up and paddle, I felt sure I could overtake her. The scheme had an air of adventure that inspired me, and the thought of the water-cask beside the fore companion doubled my growing courage.

Up I got, was greeted almost instantly by another cloud of spray, but this time stuck to my purpose and set myself, with all my strength and care, to paddle after the unsteered HISPANIOLA. Once I shipped a sea so heavy that I had to stop and bail, with my heart fluttering like a bird, but gradually I got into the way of the thing and guided my coracle through the waves, with only now and then a blow upon her bows and a dash of foam in my face.

I was now gaining rapidly on the schooner; I could see the brass glisten on the tiller as it banged about, and still no soul appeared upon her decks. I could not help but assume she was deserted. If not, the men were lying drunk below, where I might batten them down, perhaps, and do what I chose with the ship.

For some time she had been doing the worst possible thing for me — standing still. She headed nearly due south, yawing, of course, all the time. Each time she fell off, her sails partly filled, and these brought her in a moment right back to the wind again. I have said this was the worst possible thing for me, for helpless as she looked in this position, with the canvas cracking like cannon and the blocks trundling and banging on the deck, she still continued to run away from me, not only with the speed of the current, but by the whole amount of her leeway, which was naturally great.

But now, at last, I had my chance. The breeze fell for some seconds, very low, and the current gradually turning her, the HISPANIOLA revolved slowly round her center and at last presented me her stern, with the cabin window still gaping open and the lamp over the table still burning on into the day. The mainsail hung drooping like a banner. She was stock-still except for the current.
For the last little while I had even lost ground, but now redoubling my efforts, I began once more to overtake the chase.
